January Anniversaries.—The present month is not welcomed by certain members of the Royal Family, for the reason that the first month of the year holds many sad anniversaries for them. The 22nd for instance, is the anniversary of the death of our beloved Queen Victoria; the 14th is the anniversary of the death of the Duks of Clarence, and it was upon the 20th of January, eleven years ago, that Prince Henry of Batten- berg passed away. To Queen Victoria December was far more a month of ill-omen than January, but with her sound and practical good sense, she never allowed the several sad anniversaries to interfere with her duties and engagements, The Cat Show at Westminster.—Princess Victoria of Schleswig-Holstein, President of the Southern Counties Cat Club, sent four cats to the Royal Horticultural Society's Hall, last week. None of the Royal pets however won prizes, although two were highly com- mended. The Princess has a wonderful " cattery " at Cumberland Lodge and is a.great lover of the feline race. Princess Lousie of Schleswig-Holstein is also devoted to animals, cats and dogs especially, of which she owns several prize winners. The Baroness Burdett-Ooutts' Fortune.—The popular idea that the Baroness Burdett-Coutts was the richest woman in the world, was the outcome of some exaggera- tion, but in her early life there were very few really rich people compared to what there are nowadays, and it is not surprising that popular imagination should have attributed to her riches beyond those she really possessed. She never had more than a life interest in the greater part of the fortune accumulated by her grandfather, Mr. Thomas Coutts, who left it to his wife Harriet Mellon, a one-time strolling play-actress, who, as the widowed Mrs. C,outts married in 1827 the ninth Duke of St. Albans. It was under the Duchess's will that the late Baroness inherited and, owing to a pro- vision against her marrying a foreigner, she had to. sacrifice a large part of her income from the trust property, when she married Mr. Burdett-Coutts in 1881. Mr. Burdett-Contts is American born and came to this country with his brother the late Sir Ellis Ashmead Bartlett in the e.irly sixties. The Baroness of course always bad a very large income, and most of the property at her disposal she made over to Mr. Burdett- Coutte during her lifetime but the beneficiary who :succeeds under the trust, is her nephew, Mr. Francis Burdett Mona-Coutts.

General Booth's Family.—Most of General Booth's family are associated with the work of the Salvation Army, although some are separated from it. His eldest daughter, who married Mr.Clibborn, and lives in Paris, is not a Salvationist, and his son, Mr. Ballington Booth has organised a sort of rival army of his own in America. Miss Eva Booth, an unmarried daughter, is in chage of the Salvation Army forces in America,where the General_ is shortly proceeding on a visit. He is undertaking another world tour, visiting Japan, India, and other countries, althougt he will have entered upon his eightieth year before his expected return in the summer. It is generally supposed that he will be suc- ceeded, as chief of the Army by his son Mr. Bramwell Booth, whose second daughter has recently entered as a cadet at the training home at Clapton. Prevailing Modes.—There appears little doubt that extravagance and elaboration will strike the dominant note in the world of dress and fashions for 1907. The craze for having every detail of dress to match is a very expensive one, and is carried to such extremes that boots, hosiery, buttons, jewellery, handkerchief, and umbrella handle, must all accord with the gown in colour and design. This is one feature of the prevail- ing modes, and another is the apparently successful attempt to make the small waist fashionable, as it was a generation ago. It is the day of the tall and slender girl, but our long accustomed use of the blouse, the straight-fronted corset, and the vogue for outdoor exer- cise and amusements, do not make for hour-glass waists, and it will be a difficult task for Society, if she is set up as a divinity which all the world of fashion must worship. Curious Buttons.—The tailors are indulging in the most fantastic buttons, some being decidedly more curious than beautiful. Under the latter category come the buttons coveree with sealskin, and outlined with a kilted pleating of satin. Oval buttons are more favoured by leading tailors than the round varieties a a favourite design being a foundation of satin covered with a network of fine silk cord. Buttons employed upon fancy waistcoats are invariably covered with the material of which the costume is built. The Scarcity of Whalebone.--,Old umbrellas :ank with old boots as a particularly useless kind of lumber, but if they are sufficiently ancient, and of the ole whalebone ribbed variety, they have a good market valve. So scarce has whalebone become that they are eagerly bought up for the sake of their ribs, which are turned to account for other purposes. These umbrellas are till found in country cottages and out-of-the-way places, and if the whalebone is sound they are worth more than was originally paid for them. Science has improved upon Nature in many ways, but ft has not yet produced a satisfactory substitute for either whalebone or ivory, although it looks as if the whale and the elephant were both doomed to disappear as they become more and more hunted for their valuable products. The Dangers of Flannelette.—Much has been said and written lately about the dangers of cheap foreign flannelette, and yet this horrible material is still purchased and lives are sacrificed accordingly. I

The greatest possible care needs to be exercised in the purchase of flannelette, and none should be bought unless stamped in such a manner as to show it is of home manufacture. Flannelettes chemically treated so as to render them non-inflammable, are not to be recom- mended, one drawback being tendency to absorb the moisture in the atmosphere. It is quite easy to detect chemically treated flannelette by its feeling of damp- ness. A good, genuine home-made flannelette costs, it is true a few pence more per yard, but it is almost, if not quite as safe as flannel; in wear it is not to be com- pared with the foreign rubbish, and it has none of the unhealthy, disagreeable clamminess of the chemically- treated varieties.

A New Method of Telling Fortunes.—There are many Iways of telling fortunes. One of the best known is reading the hand, but in Germany the people have got tired of that decorous drawing-room method, and have adopted the less elegant fashion of telling fortunes by putting out the tongue. A long tongue, we are ,told, has not the significance we usually attach to it, but denotes an open and generous character. Its po§sessor ldom, if ever, has money in the Savings Banit The short tongue indicates the other extreme, the mean and miserly spirit. Genius and artistic temperament are shewn by a thin, quivering, tongue, and many other degrees of character are represented by certain features of the tongue. Altogether the science does not seem to have much to recommend it as a drawing-room pastime, and it has not the chief merit of palmistry in providing the excute and occasion for a little hand squeezing and innocent flirting. Poets, Artists, and Flowing Locks.—Everyone knows that musicians, poets, artists, and composers, are addicted to the long hair habit. The more eminent they are in any of these professions, the more they more they cultivate luxuriant heads of hair, and it is ft standing enigma why they should do it. Dr. Cowen dis- cusses this subject in one of the currant magazines, but he is unable to give any satisfactory explanation of this connection between flowing locks and certain pro- fessions. Lawyers and architects do not, as a rule, object to prematnre baldness, because there is a popular belief that it is evidence of great intellect powers, but why poets, pianists, violinists, and artists, should consider it necessary to cultivate extraordinary heads of hair, is apparently one of those things no one can understand.
MADGE.

div.head: HINTS FOR THE CHILDREN
div.p: HINTS FOR THE CHILDREN

Rich cakes and pastries, however tempting they may appear to young eyes, should never be allowed early in the meal. Have an abundance of thinly cut currant bread and butter upon the table and you will soon discover that nine guests out of ten heartily appreciate this tempting and truly wholesome food. Given a foundation of currant bread and butter, the child is ready to finish the meal quite appropriately with plum cake or other festal dainties.

Mr. J. Moore Murray Lectures on "Eclucatlon." At Bewsey-road Lecture Hall on Monday. evening. Mr. J. Moore Murray, M.Sc., Director of Education read to the Wesley Guild a paper on "Education." The Director dealt with the subject from the utilitarian point of view, because that appeals more directly to the majority of ratepayars. And; as he pointed out, the immaterial and infinitely more valuable results of education followed even when education had been bestowed merely because it will be useful. Mr. Murray emphatically„ stated that the "opportunity of even the poorest children should only be limited by their mental capacity." He pointed out that now the educational scheme in Warrington made it possible for a child with ability, though poor, to pass through ; the Technical School and the Grammar School, and he hoped it would soon be possible for them to go up to the universities: Referring to children of average ability, he said that now, when they left school at the age of thirteen to become wage earners, they quickly lost all that their eight years of school life had given them except the much abused power to read. While, if they I could only stay at school another couple of years, their awakening reasoning faculties c(Aild be trained, ' and their chance of doing useful, intelligent work for, the community increased ten fold. Deepest sympathy was expressed for the parents with six or more chil- dren, earning eighteen shillings a week, who took their children from school at the earliest possible opportunity. It was pointed out that until the wages of the father were raised the Education Authorities , could do little for the child. One very practical suggestion Mr. Murray made was that the elder girls 1 ' should be specially trained to become the intelligent 1 heads of households. It was ridiculous to give the , girl of twelve exactly the same lessons as the boy of twelve, and Mr. Murray suggested a course of house-! hold arithmetic, laundry work, sick-nursing, and care I of babies to be added to the present instruction 'in I cookery. Mr. Upson expressed his full agreement with the scheme proposed in the paper. Alderman : Tirion presided over the meeting.

div.head: SOME' CURRENT JEWELLERY.
div.p: SOME' CURRENT JEWELLERY.

We are going to the East and to classic days for some of our best models in jewellery, and among these, says the Queen, are magnificent diadems modelled after the Greek repousse work, and bead necklaces in dull gold, and ear- rings with tasselled ends of gold to match a similar necklace. They were worn 2,400 years ago, and figure in many of our museums. The pity is that we do not make more use of such beautiful models. Some of the small rosettes that figure on the jewels are marvellously worked", and simulate five-petalled flowers, and were no doubt originally enamel. No pains were spared, and some of the clasps are marvels of workmanship.

div.head: MODERN WOMEN BEST,
div.p: MODERN WOMEN BEST,

We are all complaining that intelligent talk- ing i% becoming 1 and less _frequent in Eng- land, yet, complains " Marmaduke " in • the Graphic, few endeavour to discover the cause of the decay. The many " Reminiscences " we possess, and other evidence, prove that the ordi- nary Englishwoman in every generation was dull in this direction; she was neither a good conversationalist, nor had she the talent of lead- ing men on to brilliant talking. Our women of to-day are undoubtedly an improvement in both respects on their predecessors, for the majority of the former are better educated, more intelli- ant, more experienced, and more confident than were the majority of the latter.

div.head: VELVETEEN BLOUSE.
div.p: VELVETEEN BLOUSE.

Velveteen blouses are among the most cosy and comfortable of garments for cold-weather wear. This year they are particularly fashion- able, and as velveteen is by no means expensive, and is obtainable in every ima- ginable shade, they make a valuable ad- dition to the winter wardrobe. The colour chosen should match exactly the skirt with which the blouse is intended to be worn— odd blouses, with the exception of white and ivory, are completely demo& for the moment.

div.p: The Examiner, oaturday, January 19, 1907. SCIENCE NOTES AND NEWS
TO DESTROY MICROBES,

Microbes cannot be killed by great violence, as large animals can, and the blow of a 100-ton steam hammer would not kill one of them. They are, however, subject to subtle forms of vio- lence, such as rotary motion, tapping, and vi- bration. Dr. Samuel ,J. Melzer placed bottles of germs in the vibratory machine of a soda-water manufacturer, and found that they were killed by the motion. The appatatus produced vibra- tion and a strong centrifugal (flying from the centre) tendency.

div.head: NEAREST TO PERPETUAL MOTION
div.p: NEAREST TO PERPETUAL MOTION

About eighty years ago Dr. Robert Brown dis- covered that microscopic particles—such as pow- dered indigo, carmine, gamboge, • &c.—keep in rapid movement when suspended in water. The peculiar oscillations may continue for years,' and seem to be, the nearest approach to perpetual motion yet observed. It occurred to Dr. Carl Herning and Dr. E. Northrup to test the influence of an electric current upon this Brownian move- ment. When the suspending liquid was placed between two electrodes, the particles took a very decided course across the field, some being attracted to one electrode and some to the other. Each particle had its characteristic direction, and in some miiitures the particles of one material travelled with the current, and those of the other against it. The motion was so posi- tive that Dr. Northrup has made it the basis of a successful electrical measuring instrument for special purposes. '

THE UNIMAGINABIIE COLD OF SPACE. We live, says Science Aiftings, under a blanket of air, which protects us from the extreme cold of outer space. This low temperature becomee evident 14,000 ft. or 15,000 ft, above the surface of the earth, and would reach a point far below zero at a height of ten miles. At this height we should no longer observe the twinkling of the stars, for the scintillation is due to the move- ments of our atmosphere, which at this height would be extremely- rarefied. If one could photo- graph the sun's spectrum at this altitude we could greatly extend our knowledge of the shortest waves lengths in light, for the atmo- sphere completely absorbs such wave lengths as are concernod in thc, X.rny_ phanomc-rra. - That this absorption really takes place can be proved in a laboratory. The heat and light which we receive from the sun are thus greatly modified by this " blanketing " layer of air. The long waves of energy from the sun are called heat waves. The intermediate waves are termed light waves, and we receive these in full measure.

div.head: POSSIBLE ABORIGINES OF AFRICA
div.p: POSSIBLE ABORIGINES OF AFRICA

An obscure 'race may possibly be the true{ aborigines of Africa south of the Zambesi. These I are the Kattea—or Vaalpens, as they are nick. named by the Boers, on account of the dusty colour their abdomen acquires from the habit of creeping into their holes in the ground—who live in the steppe region of the North Transvaal, as far as the Limpopo. •As their complexion is almost a pitch black, and their stiture only about 1.220 meters (4ft.), they are quite distinct from their tall Bantu neighbours an I from the yellowish Bushmen. The "Dogs," or "Vul- tures," as the Zulus call them, are the "lowest of the , low," being undoubtedly cannibals, and often making a meal of their own aged and iii- firm, which the Bushmen never do. Their habitations are holes in the ground, rock shel- ters, and lately a few hovels. They have no arts or industries, nor even any weapons except those obtained in exchange for ostrich feathers, skins, or ivory. Whether they have any religious ideas- it is impossible to say, all intercourse being re- stricted to barter carried on in a gesture h•n- guage, for nobody has ever yet mastered their tongue, all that is known of their language being that it is absolutely distinct from that of both the Bushman and the Bantu. There are no tribes, merely little family groups of from thirty to fifty individuals, each of which is presided over by a headman, whose functions \ are ac- quired, not by heredity, but by personal quali- ties. So little information is available concern- king the Kattea that it is impossible to say any- thing about their racial affinities.

div.head: GROWTH OF " RADIOBES."
div.p: THE GROWTH OF " RADIOBES."

Some time ago Mr. Douglas Rudge, repeating the experiments of Mr. Butler Burke on the action of radium on gelatin, came to the conclu- sion that the " radiobes" were simply precipi- tates of barium sulphate, and not in any sense living organisms. Mr. Budge continued hie work, and embodied his results in a paper which was communicated to the Royal Society by Professor J. J. Thomson. He finds that a " growth " appears when radium compounds are placed in contact with gelatin, and that it has a cellular structure. This is due, however, he contends, to the barium, always associated with radium salts, forming an insoluble precipitate with the sulphuric acid always present in com- mercial gelatin. When specially purified gelatin containing no trace of sulphuric acid is used radium gives no "growth." Some radium salt sealed up with gelatin free from sulphuric acid for eight months shewed no: signs of cellular growth. Mr. Rudge concludis that radium has no specific action in forming cells, any effect pro- duced being due to the presence of barium in the sample. The purer samples of radium are ob- served to produce less effect than the impure., Pure radium salts would probably produce no action except an evolution of gas. The cellular form of the precipitate is ex- plained by Mr. Rudge -to be due to the fact that tho gelatin is liquefied, and that each particle of precipitate is formed round a core of gelatin. Thus a 10er of barium sulphate forms a sort of sac, or cell, which is surrounded by a solution of the radium salt in liquefied gelatin. This "cell" may be permeable to s the solution, which passitig in causes it to swell. The dells do not divide or bud, and their growth quickly reaches a maximum.

div.head: VAGARIES OF WELLS.
div.p: THE VAGARIES OF WELLS.

According to the observation of M. Grosse- teste upon some of the wells which are situated in the canton of Geneva, it appears that the wells have the remarkable property of drawing in air at certain times and of blowing out air at other periods. These wells are considered by the inhabitants of these districts as very exact indi- cations of the weather. When the wells blow out air, it is a sign that rain is to follow, and when air is drawn in, it is a sure indication of fine weather. Since the wells are covered with a flat stone having , a hole in it, according to the cus- tom of the region, it is easy to observe the direc- tion which is taken by the current of air. Some observers installed upon one of the wells a pres- sure-gauge of U-form, and were thus able to find some interesting points about the air-currents. Thus they find that a well is seldom in a state of equilibrium. It blows out air when the barometer falls, and sucks in air when it rises. These variations do not exceed *a height of one, inch on the gauge. As to the theory of the action of these wells it is to be remarked that they lie in strata of alluvial gravel covered with vegetable earth which is quite or nearly imper- vious .to water. We may therefore admit that, owing to the spaces which exist between the stones of the gravel, these strata form a reser- voir of great capacity in which the water cir- culates. Tho water comes into the cavities when the atmospheric pressure is lowered, and it leaves them when the pressure rises. The effect of these movements is thus felt within the well, in- asmuch as the latter forms the connecting point with tho outer air. This phenomenon may be said to have a -considerable analogy—with _the emission of gases by certain hot springs to caves where a current of air circulates upon the ground, to the variations in the flow of springs, 1 and other phenomena of a like 'nature.
THE PREVAILING INFLUENZA.

Whether the influenzal epidemics recorded in history were of the same kind as the modern disease is extremely doubtful, says a Hospital writer. For practical purposes, what we now call by that name is, among Europeans, a new disease. , An exceptional interest attaches, there- fore, to _ the phenomena attending its establish- ment among us, and particularly to that extreme variability of type which characterises it. There is a struggle for existence among diseases, and those which establish themselves among us do 1 so in proportion to a power of adaptability which is expressed in Darwinian phrase as the "sur- vival of the fittest." What, from the clinical standpoint, might be called the evolution of in- fluenza, from its primitive pyrexial to its pre- sent modified type among adults, throws some light on a question of interest in regard to the general theory of immunity. What is the reason that • a person who has been the victim of nume- rous attacks of inflaviza seldom, if ever; displays the same symptoms in, successive illnesses? If one year the attack has been attended by acute pharyngitis or tonsillitis, next year it may be ushered in by acute abdominal_ pain with or without diarrhcei. and vomiting, possibly culmi- nating in appendicitis or a mild form of general peritonitis. Or, again, there may be headache of agonising severity, suggestive of meningeal in- flaminSion as the pathological basis. Re- cently, a tendency to ophthalmic complications, conjunctivitis, blepharitis, even glaucoma, has becn forced upon my recognition. Surely this ettreme variability, with an unvarying substra- tum of general -toxcemic symptoms too character- istic to be easily overlooked, is in a high degree gue-&.:estive of a urridulal exhaustion of the suscen- tibility of particular tissues and organs—the de- velopment of local immunities which narrow ' down the field of action of the batillus and its toxines.

div.p: HARRIERS.
WARRINGTON A.C. v. WIDNES UNITED.

The return inter-club race between these two clubs took place on Saturday last at Widnes. The hares J. Hall and W. Unsworth (Warrington) along with two locals were despatched at 3 o'clock, and they laid an eight mile trail through Ditton, Hough Green, Spring- field, Crouton and Farnwortb, back to headquarters. The pack consisting of 14 of Warrington and 12 Widnes followed thirty minutes later, and after an absence of fifty minutes, the first man appeared in sight, who turned out to be J. Parsonage, Warrington, who was an easy winner, the others followed in close order. The result being an easy win for Warrington. Score :

div.head: WARRINGTON WESLEYAN HARRIERS..
div.p: WARRINGTON WESLEYAN HARRIERS..

On Saturday the above Club received a visit from the Manchester Gymnasium (Y.M.C.A.) Harriers. 'Owing to the visitors arriving late, it was past the hour of four when a start was made. Trail had been laid over about seven miles of very heavy country in the Bewsey and Burtonwood district, and after a hard run, victory rested with the Warrington team by 25 points to 75. The individual honours were also taken by two Wesleyans, C. Vose leading all the way and winning with ease from J. Massey, who was closely follotred by C. P. Rodwell, of Manchester, who travelled at a stiffish pace for the last two miles of the race. A medal to be given to the first novice to arrive home was won by T. Conroy, IWesleyans, who, running well all through the race, was not far behind Rodwell at the finish. A little excite- ment was caused when it was found that three runnel* two from Manchester and one from Warrington, had missed the trail, and owing to darkness it was feared that they might not be able to find the dressing-rooms, and search parties were sent out. However, they eventually arrived about half an hour later. After the run the visitors were entertained to tea at the Lecture Hall, Bewsey-road Chapel, and a very enjoyable evening followed. The programme was practically filled by the Y.M.C.A. members,C. T. Dickenson (captain) leading off with a humorous recitation entitled" Snorkins," which caused great amusement, Songs by Messrs. Foulkes Nowack. Hartley (Manchester), were interpersed with humorous recitals by Mr. Dickenson, and a reading on the Indian Mutiny by Mr. Hartley. Mr. T. Attwell (Warrington), was encored for his song "The song that the Anvil sings" and followed with" Drinking "and "The Diver." Messrs. H. and C. Sinclair sang with great effect as a duet "Larboard Watch." Mr. W. Martin was the accompanist, and great credit is due to him, as he was called on without previous warning. Refreshments were served at, about 9.30 p.m. as the visitors had to be away early, owing to several living a distance out of Manchester. The singing of "Auld lang Syne " terminated what was considered by all, a very enjoyable evening.

Ragged School and Mission. On Sunday evening the limelight serviCe was con- ducted by Mr. Robert Cade. The subject was "The life of St. Paul" and the slides were most instructive. Miss S. A. Titchard sweetly sang "Art thou weary." Mr. Blakemore was the accimpanist and the lantern was manipulated by Mr. F. Owen. Death of Mr. William Horton. The death took place at his residence, Wilderspool- causeway, on Monday, of Mr. William Horton. The deceased gentleman, who was 48 years of age, had been a director of Henry-Milling and Co. for about 25 years. Mr. Horton, who was much respected, was at the shop no later than Wednesday last. He had been ailing for some time, but his death was quite unexpected. He leaves a widow and three children. Death of Mrs. Ivan Fulton-Smith. We record with deep regret the sudden and unexpected death of Mrs. Ivan FrOton-Smith, which took Place at the residence of her parents (Councillor and Mrs. Nield), 18, Salisbury-street, on Sunday. The deceased lady, who bad only been married about twelve Months, was a daughter in-law of Councillor Fulton-Smith, and was. deeply respected by a large circle of friends,by whom her death is much regretted. Great sympathy has been extended to the bereaved husband and parents, in the sad loss they have sustained. LADIES' BEST GLACE BOOTS AND SHOES, UNDER THE CLOCK, BRIDGE-STREET.—AdtV. Loyal Order of Ancient Shepherds. On Saturday the 12th of January 1907 the quarterly meeting of the Warrington District was held at the Rose Bud Lodge, St. James' schoolroom, Latchford, under the presidency_of Pro. C. S. Bro. Thomas Baskerville. He was supported by Trustees Bros. William Hall and William Eckersley, District Treasurer, Bro. James Parr; District Secretary, Bro. Peter Edgar, and delegates from the various Lodges belonging to such District. The President in opening the meeting wished all both collectively and individu- ally "A happy and prosperous New 'Year." At the request of the Chief the District Secretary read the accounts for quarter endidg 31st December last, and on the auditors (Bros. Haley and Gresty), having certified their correctness the same were unanimously passed. At the same meeting the Secretary presented the annual statement of accounts of Lodges and Dis- trict for the year 1906. The District Examiner (Brc s. Weir and Harris) also read their reports upon such. accounts. After a short discussion the accounts and remrts were passed as satisfactory. PUBLIC BENEFIT, UNDER Tile CLOCK FOR BERT BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Parr's Bank. The annual meeting of Parr's Bank, Limited, will be held at the Cannon-street Hotel, London, on Thurs- day next. In their annual report the direc+ors state that the positicm and prospects of the business COR- tinue to be in every way satisfactory. Including £119,785 4s, 3d. brought forward at 30th June, 1906, the net balance of profits for the half-year, after pro- viding for all bad and doubtful debts, and rebating the current bills at 6 per cent. is .042,175 12s. Bd. From thie sum the directors recom- mend the payment of a ball-year's dividend at the rate of 19 per cent per annum (M 62,207 10s.) a bonus of one per cent (£17,085), 'the transfer to bank premises account of £lO,OOO and the transfer to officers' pension and provident fund of £ls,ooo,leaving a balance to be carried to the next account of £137,783 2s. Bd. The retiring directors the Hon. Sir C. W. Fremantle, K.C.8., Sir David Gamble, Bart.,K.C.B. Mr. John Dun, Mr. Edward W. Nix, Mr. Edward Banbury, and Mr. Robert Neill, are eligible for re-election. During the yeas a branch bank has been opened at St. John's-road,Waterloo,Liverpool . VVOOD CHIMNEY PIECES, Fite Grates and Tiles. nrivalled sele tion, inspection invited.—J. S. UGARLAND, Builders' *lronmonger, &c., 51 to 55, Bridge at., Warrington.—Advt. Shorthand Writers' Association. There was a good attendance at the weekly meeting of this Association, held at the Winmarleigh Cafe on Wednesday night. Speed practice (to which special attention is now being given in view of the spring. examinations), was conducted in two sections, at fairly .high and low rates. Miss E. Houghton then read a thoroughly enjoyable paper entitled: "How to succeed as a Typist." In her opening remarks she trusted that it would not be considered presumptiqn on her part if she stated that the paper had been written in the light of practical experience. In referr- ing to a typist's qualifications, the lecturer 'considered that it was of the utmost importance that such clerks should be possessed of capability and adaptability, and should extend courtesy to all. It was also very essential that enthusiasm be put into one's work, to which should be given full consideration, in order that justice might be done to anything that the typist was called upon to undertake. Miss Houghton urged that every opportunity be taken of studying commercial subjects—especially languages—so that in due time the typist might,by her or his own knowledge and zeal, rise to a more responsible (and, she hoped, lucrative) position. The 'paper was listened to with great atten- tion.—A vote of thanks to Miss Houghton terminated the meeting. PUBLIC BENEFIT.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. Charge of Embezzlement. At the Liverpool County Sessions on Tuesday, Harry Parrott (34), described as a commission agent, was charged with having embezzled £5 ss. belonging to the British Soap Powder Co., nn 'the 2nd of July; and with having embezzled a further, sum of £5 2s. 6d. on July 7th. Mr. A. Hyslop Maxwell and Mr. H. Lindon Riley prosecuted, and Mr. W. Madden was for defence.—The British Soap Powder Co until June last had their works in Warwickshire, and in that month removed to Warrington. In March, according to the prosecution, the prisoner was engaged as traveller in the Midland district at a salary of £2 per week and £2 weekly expenses. It was alleged that he had received two amounts of £5 ss. and £5 2s. 6d. from two customers in Birmingham, for which he had never accounted to his employers.—The defence was that the prisoner was never the servant of the prosecuting company. He had acted simply as agent, and he had never done any work for them on any other terms than that of 10 per cent. commission. There was a balance qf £57 due to him by the company, and he had held the cash in hand against their account. One of the payments embraced in the charge was disputed by the prisoner, who gave evidence on his own behalf.— The hearing of the case lasted for four hours and a half, and the correspondence between the prisoner and the firm lonized the subject of long armngenta —A verdict of "Not guilty" was agreed upon by the jury, and Parrott was discharged. " HERALD " KITCHEN RANGES and " Peveril " Fire Grates are hard to beat.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge s.t., Warrington.—Advt. Visit of Wingates Temperance Band. Warrington people were on Sunday afforded an opportunity of hearing the famous Wingates Temper- ance Band which by its victory at the Crystal Palace last year holds the brass band championship of Great Britain. Two concerts were given in the Parr Hall, the proceeds being devoted to the Runcorn, Warring- ton and Widnes Grappling Corps, of which Mr. W. Byfield is the superintendent. It was gratifying to see that there were large attendances and this deserv- ing object should benefit by the effort. In the after- noon an excellent programme was submitted and all who attended were warm in their admiration of the performances of the band. The members responded to the baton as one man and every attention was paid to detail and expression, an organ-like effect being pro- duced in many of the more beautiful passages. The stirring" Tancredi " overture was a fitting opening item and the admirable tendering roused the audience to the highest' appreciation. Not less pleasing was the " Verdi "selection (arranged by Round) but the thief item was the prize piece " Poliuto " (Donizetti) by which the band has won over £2OO. The playing was indeed brilliant and all the solo parts were well sustained. The air vane "Austrian Hymn" (Swift) was artistically given. Special mention should be made of a cornet solo by Mr. Pollard who displayed. remarkable skill. The programme was varied by several vocal items. Miss Ethel Parr, a well-known Eisteddfod prize winner, sang with much feeling "Nearer my God to Thee" and " The Better Land, while Mr. Walter Shaw, a baritone medallist with a pleasing voice, interpreted " Thou'rt passing hence" and "The way of peace" with good effect. Mr. A. E. Trow was an able accompanist Selections on the mandoline by the 'Sisters Vera (late with Brogden's Swiss Choir) proved an enjoyable feature of the concert. The evening programme was equally interesting and called forth many eulogiums. The band selections included the difficult piece "Gems from Chopin "for their rendering of which Wingates secured the championship trophy at the last Crystal Palace contest.

Warrington & District Cricket League Formed. At a meeting on ruesday evening it was decided that a cricket league be formed under the above name. There was a good attendance of representatives of the junior clubs, Mr. W. Podmore, the Warrington secre- tary, presiding. Mr. J. WoAhead., 24, Oldham-strpet, was appointed secretary. An early meeting bf the secretaries of all com'peting „clubs is to be held. There is every prospect of the League being a great

success. . • Sand of Hope Concert. On Monday evening a successful entertainment in connection with the Buckley-street Sunday School Band of Hope Society was held. Recitations were given by Miss Emily Vale and Willie Forster; solos by Miss Nellie Lomax, Miss Ada Whalley, Miss Jane Harrison and Mr. J. Urmston ; duets by the Misses Whalley and Harrison, and Harrison and La-max, and a reading by Mr. John Oultram. - Mr- A.

Jennings presided. Popular Penny Concert. There was a crowded attendance at Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom on Saturday. evening at the weekly concert. Songs were rendered by the Misses Lena Duckworth, May Isherwood, Emily Millard, Avice Beswick, a.nd Pattie Taylor, and Messrs. S. Hassan, James Hardy, R. Johnson and Levi Richard- son. The Misses Duckworth and Taylor were warmly applauded for a well-rendered duet. The humorous element was in the, hands of Mr. J. Robinson, of Runcorn, who caused much amusement with his witty sayings. The accompanists were Miss Gibson and Mr. Levi Richardson. Catholic Dance The third annual dance in connection with the Warrineton Catholic Young Men's Society was held on Taesday evening in the Parr Hall, when about 150 members and their friends were present. The music was in the hands of Mr. A. Starkey, and the dancing, which commenced ot S p.m., and finished at 2 a,.m„ was thoroughly enjoyed, the programme containing 22 attractive items. Mr. T. Newns proved an efficient M.C., and he was ably Assisted by an energetic com- mittee with kfessrs. M. Cunningham andreter Delaney as Sacretaries. The refreshments were supplied by a committee of ladies and gave great satisfaction. -- Spiritualism. Warrington Spiritualists were on Sunday favoured by a visit from Mr. A. Wilkinson, a noted clairvoyant and clairaudient medium, of Holdsworth, near Halifax. In the evenin„e• the hall was crowded, when Mr. Wilkinson dealt with questions from the audience, the principal being" What is the object of life? " and What is the ultimate destiny of the soul'?" The first formed the basis for a capital address; as to the second,though there might be speculation, and though there was evidence of progression towards that per- fection which was one orthe objects of life,there could be no certainty,-as to‘the sonl'S final destiny. A clair- voyant exhibition followed: On Monday evening the hall was again crowded when Mr. Wilkinson spoke on "The natare of our evidences." Fire in the Market-place. Shortly after eight o'clock on Tuesday morning. a fire broke out in the lock-up shop of Mr. Fie d Falshaw, glass merchant and picture frame manufac- turer, Market-place. P.O 's Tolley and Turner at once proceeded to the shop. The fire brigade was summoned and Superintendent Turner was quickly on the scene with a reel cart. Owing to the fire at Earlestown, which had broken out several hours previously, few firemen were left in Warrington, and it is a fortunate circumstance, therefore, that the Superintendent and the police arrived in time to be able to cope with the flames, which it appears, had broken out in the back part of the cellar. Some straw and pieces of wood ignited, but the flames were soon extinguished. In the cellar there were several barrels containing paraffin oil, and had these become ignited the outbreak would have assumed serious proportions. As it was very little damage was done. STRANGE'S A.l. Crystal LAMP OIL in barrels or drums delivered free.—Sole agent, J. S. GARLAND, 51 to 55, Bridge st., Warrington.—Advt. Crimean Veteran's Death, Another Crimean and Indian Mutiny veteran passed away on Wednesday of last week in the person of William Spruce, aged 71 years, who died in the Withington Workhouse Hospital, where he had been suffering for some two months from cancer in the mouth. A native of Appleton Thorn, near Warrington, Spruce for the last 26 years had been a familiar figure in Altrincham. He spent about 17 years in the .rmy, and went through the Crimea and the Indian Mutiny. He was for 12} years in the 51st foot regiment. He received a pension of 74. a day, but on November 7th last it was raised to is. through the efforts of the Crimea and Indian Mutiny Veterans' Association, and he also received ss. a week from the Veterans' Association. The deceased's remains were laid to rest at the Southern Cemetery, Manchester, on Saturday. The coffin which was covered with a Union Jack, was conveyed to the grave on a gun carriage, 'which, by the courtesy of Major Dodgson, was sent from Hulme Barracks. Preceding the gun carriage was Inspector Knott and two members of the police force. The mourners were : —Mr. W. Spruce and Mr. G. Spruce, Sons; Mrs. C. Jackson, daughter; Mr. C. Jackson, son-in-law; Mr. G-. W. Jackson, Miss Emily Jackson and Miss Elsie Jackson, grandchildren. A number of • Army veterans also attended. Rechabite Prize Distribution. The members of the John Dimond juvenile tent of the Order of Rechabites turned up in 'full force at a meeting on Wednesday evening, at which the prizes won during the year were distributed. The proceed- ings took place in the Friars-green schoolroom, and were under the presidency of Councillor Clegg. The first business was the election of officers, and this resulted as follows :—Chief Ruler, H. Johnson; Deputy Chief Ruler, Elsie Jones ; Levite, H. Jolley; Guardian, A 2. Yates; Steward, R. Clegg; and Secretary, S. Gallop.—ln his annual report, the Secretary said the year had been fairly satisfactory. They commenced with a membership of 197, and during the year 33 new members had been initiated. Twenty-five had, however, lapsed, and as they had also lost by transference to the adult tent and by death the year closed with a member- ship of 195. Financially they had increased a balance in hand from £lB to £23.—The Rev.C.Harvey Cook, in presenting the prizes, urged the children to live up to what they professed by belonging to the Reehabite Order.—A large number of prizes for good attendance and good conduct at tent meetings were distributed and the proceedings were rendered additionally interesting by the presentation of a hand- some sash to Bro. Massey in recognition of his 15 lyears service as treasurer.—During the evening songs and recitations were given by the children and at the close oranges were distributed. TABLE, FLOOR, AND HANGING LAMPS in large orariety. Latest patterns.—J. S. GARLAND, Iron- monger Bridge St., Warrington.—Advt. Druids' Annual Meeting.

The annual District Committee meeting in connec- tion with the Warrington District of the Order of Druids was held on Saturday at the Chapel House Inn, at the invitation of the " Penketh United" Lodge, when there were present : - Bro. John Woods, District Master; Bro. G-. Henry Houghton, D.D.M. ; Bro. Robert Perdue, D.T. ; Bro. Edwin Allen, DAIS.; Bro. William Bibby, George Roughley and Samuel Hankey, trustees; and delegates from the 13 lodges comprising this district.—The Secretary submitted the annual balance sheet which showed a net gain on the year's. working of £l7O. During the past year £769 had been I paid out to members for sick benefit, and £270 for funeral benefits. Permission was given to the trustees 1 to invest £250 on freehold property at 4 per cent., bringing the total so invested up to £2,300. A long 'discussion took place as to the advisability of estab- lishing a compensation . fund for the Warrington District, and it was ultimately decided to be imprac- ticable, but the delegates were asked to recommend to their respective lodges to continue to receive the Penny per quarter . from their members for the purpose of establishing a benevolent fund to be administered by their own lodges apart altogether from the registered district funds. The following officers were elected for the next twelire months : —Bro. George Hew Houghton, District Master ; Bro. John Jackson, jun., Deputy District Master; Bro. Robert Perdue, District Treasurer; Bro. Edwin Allen, District Corresponding Secretary : Bro. John Gillin, junior auditor. The business meet- ing over, the delegates and visiting brothers adjourned to the dining-room f where -a substantial tea had been provided by Mr. William Unsworth, the landlord. Ultimately a successful social was presided over by the newly-elected District Master, Bro. G. H. Houghton. Toasts were _honoured and the following brethren enlivened the proceedings with songs :-- A. Goulden, John Jankson, Peter Derbyshire, A. Shaw, Walter Ray, and W. H. Ireland, Bro. H. Afainley was very successful in his recitation. Selec- tions were also given on the gramophone. A hearty vote of thanks to the artistes, Host and Hostess, and Chairman for presiding was proposed by Bro. R. E. • Pooley and carried unanimously.

div.head: ODBFELLOWS ANNUAL MEETING.
div.p: ODBFELLOWS ANNUAL MEETING.

The annual meeting of the Independent Order of Oddfellov, Manchester Unity (Warrington District} was held on Saturday at the Admiral Nelson" Lodge, Pelican Hotel., Warrington, Prow. G. M. Thomas P. Bradshaw presiding over a full comple- ment of delegates from the various lodges. The accounts for the quarter ending 31st December 1900 disclosed a gain to the District Funeral Fund of £57 2s. Bd. after paying funeral benefits amounting to £9O, while the accounts for the year showed a gain to the fund of £254 17s. 81 after the pay- ment cif £4OO for funeral benefits, the fund now being £2,820 7s. 7d. This was considered satisfactory and the accounts were duly passed. N. G. W. Bibb Y (Admiral Nelson Lodge) was elected auditor. The meeting having considered the valua- tion of and the report of the actuaries on the funeral fund and as the same showed good progress it was• resolved that it be received. P.G. Geo. F. Freeman and P.G. A. E. Spann were appointed lodge book examiners and then followed the election of four representatives to attend the meeting of the Lanca- shire and' Adjacent Districts Conference at Bootie on February 10th, Prow. G.l. T. P. Bradshaw, Prow.. D.G.M. W. Holbrbok., P.G. T. P. Forbes and P.G. J. A. Wright being appointed. The meeting decided to be represented at the A.M.C. at Folkestone by two deputies and P.P G.M. Ellis R. Clare and P.G. Walter Knowles were elected as such deputies. The election of officers was the next item and Prov.D.G.M. William Holbrook was unanimously elected to fill the position of Prow. G.il. There were three nominations- for the office of Prow. D.G.M. but as two of the candidates retired P.G. Lot Brooks of tbe Navigation Lodge, Cadishead, had the unani-- mous support of the meeting for the office. The offices of Examining and Relieving Officer and Sick Visitor were filled without opposition, the retiring officers P.G. A.E. Smithson and P.G. George Higham being re-elected. There was a poll for the office of Grand Tyler and P.P.G.M. John. H. Norbury was electecr The retiring Prow. G.M. then impressively installed Bro. William Holbrook as Prow. Grand Master and Bro. Lot Brooks as Prov. Deputy Grand Master and those officers suitably responded. Bro. Holbrook having taken the chair the meeting unani- mously decided to , present Bro. Bradshaw with a Past Prow. Grand Master's Gold Jewel suitably inscribed, in recognition of his services as Prow. G.M. the same to be presented to him at the complimentary dinner which is being given to him by his Lodge, (the Prince of Wales Lodge) on February 7th. A most successful meettng was then brought to a close with the usual votes of thanks.

A girl of 14 was fined ss. and costs at Ashton on Wednesday for drunkenness. At a Salvation Army meeting at Bath on Sunday a man confessed that he had been a burglar and had broken into houses at Bradford. Later he gave himself up to the police, and on Wednesday was before the Bradford Stipendiary Magistrate charged with breaking into a house at Tye:sal and stealing £l5. He was I remanded.

div.head: TETE EXAMINER.
div.p: TETE EXAMINER.
JANUARY 19th 1907.
" What is truth ? said

IS IT HERESY? jesting Pilate." That is probably the most familiar sentence that BACON ever wrote. A question as pertinent to our own times would be, " What is heresy ?" The answer that would be given to-day would be founded on a vastly greater number of considerations than would have been taken into account from thirty to forty years ago. The almost universal point of view has changed since then. It is safe to say that Bishop COLENSO would not have been persecuted for his views on the Pentateuch, and that the Rev. CHARLES VOYSEY'S drift towards Unitarianism would not have led to his exclusion from the pulpits of the Established Church. Even at that time much depended on the manner in which opinions were put forward. Dean STANLEY made a commotion by permitting Bishop COLENSO to preach in Westminster Abbey. Mr. VOYSEY, though he waa a man of uaually quiet manners, assumed a fighting pose in the pulpit, and therefore had to be suppressed so far as the Church Establishment could suppress. Had things been otherwise, had COLENSO, and then VOYSEY failed to attract any largo amount of notice, they might have continued as good Churchmen to the end.

It is contended among a more recent school of thinkers, or perhaps, we should say of Church apologists, that the Establishment ought to repre- sent all possible shades of doctrine—that, in fact, only on that condition can it be called a national Church. This is plausible; and that the Established Church does contain all shades of doctrine is doubtless true ; but such a condition of things is certainly one for which no provision has been made in the Thirty-Nine Articles. In Congregationalism, of which the Rev. R. J. CAMPBELL is a foremost representative, there is a wider scope without so much liability to transgression. There are no Thirty-Nine Articles here. Congregationalism is not a body of doctrine ; but a working agreement among I individual Churches. The minister here is in no way bound to preach the doctrine of the pastor of another place. There may be broad and wide differences. All that is expected—and even that is no enforced—is that there shall be agreement on the essential features of Christianity. But

what are these essential features? It is precisely in the answer to that question that most theo- logical difficulties arise. Mr. CAMPBELL, whose views are at present the topic of so much heated discussion, will doubtless contend that. from the teaching of the essential features of Christianity he has swerved in no way whatever. His :on ten- Con, as we understand it, is that he has given a new interpretation to them. Even this is denied by some eminent Bibical scholars and theologians, who say that Mr. CAMPBELL'S views are so little new that they are in the stage of passing into the , trite and common-place. We do not propose to enter here into the dis- cussion of vexed theological questions. But there is one aspect of the matter on which comment seems quite fair and reasonable. It is raised inci- dentally by Dr. GUINNESS ROGERS, who is nbt merely surprised by Mr. CAMPBELL'S views, but still more surprised that they should come from a man in his position. Why? The City Temple has always been somewhat indeterminate from the theological point of view. Dr. PARKER in his time raised many alarms and made many excursions ; but on the broadest questions of all he remained pretty firmly anchored. What seems to strike most of his critics is that Mr. CAMPBELL has drifted away from his anchorage, and is seeking some accidental mooring-place ; and to the plain man this seems not merely remarkable, but beyond justification. A man is appointed pastor, let us say, because he has something to teach which is agreeable to the members of his flock. He is a lighthouse shed ding illumination from a dangerous pinnacle of rock Suppose his condition to change from that of a steady revolving light to that of a will-o'- the-wisp, then, amongst those who have watched him and depended on him, there is clearly reason for a great deal of dismay and astonishment. It is the general opin- ion of mankind, we believe, that a man who preaches from a pulpit should have a settled faith, something that is very real to himself and that he finds dependable. If he permits it to be seen that instead of teaching a religion as to which he has made up his mind he is seeking some religion that he can make up his mind about, then, if he is influential at all, he makes a mental dis- turbance over a wide area, and this may be healthy or not, according to the character of his former teaching. Whether he is heretical or not depends on a great deal. To be heretical is merely to differ with the orthodox; but there are some orthodoxies that are all wrong together.
Wa are glad to notice that

FUTURE the teachers of Warrington HEADMASTERSHIPS. are not going to content themselves with merely grumbling at the preference of an outside appli- cant ovee the seventeen local men who applied for the headmastership of the Beamont School. Their representative on the Education Committee, Mr. John Upson, will move on Monday " Tuat it be an instruction to the Managers of all Council schools that, in the appointment of head teachers, the selection shall be made from among teachers serving in schools within the County Borough of Warrington." This is a drastic resolution, but it is on all fours with the attitude taken up by greater Municipal Education Authorities than that of Warrington. It is a generally accepted rule to give the preference to local men, and seeing the way the Warrington teachers were cold,thouldered on a recent occasion it is perhaps just as well to make it impossible for the school managers to import head masters from other towns, though we do not like to see the area of selection cut down too rigidly. We have enough capable teachers in Warrington to supply the demand of the new schools for some time to come and we hope Mr. Upson's resolution will become operative.

Some interesting questions THE COLONIAL have arisen in connection CONFERENCE. with the Colonial Confer- ence which is to meet in London during the coming year. The dissatisfac- tion of the Australian States has already been dealt with by the Colonial Office. Sir Clem3nt Kinloch-Cooke now puts forwards a plel that the proceedings of the Conference should be to some extent made public. He declares that Mr. Chamberlain made an error in 1897 in abandoning the principle of verbatim reports which had obtained previously—an error which he repeated in 1902. There is a good deal to be said for this view. The proceedings of the Conference, if they are to be of the utmost use to the Empire, should be available for the criticism of those publicists and politicians who are excluded from it although they are deeply interested in the questions of Imperial import which are under discussion. The ability of the Premiers and Ministers who form the gathering to voice the opinions of their several States cannot be questioned; but they must of necessity be restricted to some Went by their own predilections. And, in any case, those outside cannot judge rightly of the conclusions at which they arrive without access to the views they have expressed, and the opportunity of weighing all the considerations put forward on either side in any particular question. It is not suggested that the Conference should be open for a daily report—the conditions of daily journalism demand a style of report which might be prejudicial to, Imperial interests—but there is a good case for the full record to be preserved and issued to the public in a Blue Book.
There is a real need for THE TEMPERANCE temperancs effort in War- MissiON. rington, and those who

have been foremost in com- bating the drink evil have realized only too keenly the uphill nature of the task with which they are confronted. It is therefore with pleasure that we learn that the temperance mission conducted during the past week by Mrs. Jennie Walker has been attended with a large measure of success., To some, such efforts may savour of "preaching to the converted " but there is every reason to believe that the present „mission has . been the melthireir -readhing many -cif the class to whom it is desired to appeal. -No fewer than 150 pledges have already been taken and the mission must also have a far wider influence in that it will have stimulated and encouraged ardent temper- ance workers in their crusade. The International Order of Good Templars—a powerful and active organization which promoted the meetings—was fortunate in securing such an excellent missioner as Mrs. Jennie Walker. She has a command- ing personality, speaks with rare fluency and force, and is endowed with the dramatic instinct. By sound argument and indisput- able facts,as well as by touching anecdotes of the havoc wrought by drink, she made out an exceedingly strong CdSO for total abstinence as being the only safe aid right course. Her addresses created a deep impression and we hope that lasting good will result.
Mr. Stead in the "Review

• A SHORT WAY Of Reviews" summarises WITH THE PEERS. his proposals for dealing with the House of Lords, which will be found set forth at length in his forthcoming book" Peers or People." The Liberal majority in the House of Commons, he points out, have ready to their hand a simple, effective, and practical method of reducing the House of Peers to order, without having recourse to the drastic method of swamping the House with newly created Peers. He say: the road is clear for a Ministry bent upon removing this great obstacle from the path of progress. I suggest that at the beginning of next Session addresses should be moved to the Crown in both Houses of Parliament calling upon the Sovereign to cancel the writ of

summons issued to any Pear who could not prove that he had attended at least ten tones (luring the last Ssssiou of P:4rha.aset. Yu) iminher of attendances to be insistel upon tnight possibly be placed much higher chat) ten, hat:, let it sand at that. The justification fur waking slice a demand lies in the tact that Lird. Silishary arid Lord , Carnarvon, with the sup[?Ort of the House of Lords, recognised the desiral-Ality of addressing the Crown for the purpose of riddee4 tneir douse of persons guilty of discreditahl9 conduct incon- sistent with the po,ition of a 104islator. Can any conduct be more discreditable than that of Peers who ignore the conlinitud of their Sovereign, and fail to attend in their places in Parliament where they have been summoned? Tnese absentee Peers are guilty of a gross neglect and a breach of trust by treating the command of the Sovereign with contempt. If this is not discreditable conduct, it would be interesting to know what deserves such a description. We should •then have at one stroke reduced the House of Lords from an unmanageable body of six hundred Peers and Bishops to a small body of, say, two hundred members, to whom should be added at once a couple of hundred life Peers,whose writs of summons would, however, be liable to be cancelled or withheld if they followed the evil example of the hereditary Peers awl neglected to perform the duties for which they were summoned to Westminster.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
Mr. Keir Hardie is our greatest living statesman. Mrs. Bruce Glasier says so.
* * "I've a great deal to be thankful for," said an old woman in the almshouse. "I've two teeth left, and they're opposite each other." Such is true optimism. —" Tribune." * * *
On additional pianos for the elementary schools of London the Education Committee is expending £2,500. Think what this means for future generations of suffering neighbours. _ _

The Beautiful Warrington Society is having another tree-planting day next Thursday. In its efforts to convert Church-street into a boulevard, however, the society will be faced with considerable difficulties.

* * The attempt of the Metropolitan local authorities in conference to abolish the nuisance caused by traction engines and trailers will have the hearty support of all sufferers. At present the hideous racket caused by these things is an outrage—and not unknown in the provinces. * „

Mr. Philip Snowden, M.P., is one of the best speakers the Independent Labour Party possesses and he was listened to with great interest at 'Warrington on Saturday. Somewhat ascetic in appearance, he shows a firm grip of his subject, and possesses a fine flow of language. * *_*

"The gross misuse of authority shown in the scale of fares on the L.C.C. trains, by which the clerk is charged just three times as much as the 'workman,' will do more to kill the catch-cry of Socialism with the former section of the community than whole Niagaras of wordy argument." —" London Opinion?' _ _

The visit of the Right Hon. Sydney Bnxton, M.P., Postmaster-General, will be the occasion of a great Liberal demonstration. Quite a number of M.P.'s have promised to attend the meeting to support this prominent member of the British Cabinet. * * *

In an able article the " Lancet " points out that cold mutton is unwholesome. It is understood that the circulation of our contemporary has been largely increased, a number of men having already sent marked copies anonymously to their wives.—" Evening News" (London). * * *

Although the Rev. E. Vaughan, the popular incum- bent of Emmanuel Church, is one of the busiest of men, he is ready to assist Christianising efforts in other localities. Commencing on February 18th, he is to conduct a mission in connection with St. John's Church, Upton Manor, London, and as he is a ready and persuasive speaker, the effort should prove a success.

411 Impromptu examinations are often productive of amusing replies. On Wednesday the Rev. C. Harvey Cook was catechising the members of the John Dimond juvenile tent of Rechabites, as to the origin of the Order. Asking what the correct title would be if the old Hebrew spelling had been maintained he was astonished and amused when an enterprising youngster cried out "Please Sir, Jacobites." o _ _

So many ofthe public were anxious to attend the Co-operative Society's lecture on Thursday evening that in a remarkably short time the hall was crowded and the doors had to be closed. We wonder if the fact that free samples of cocoa &c., were to be distributed was at all accountable for the great interest shown in the meeting ? If so the promoters of the University Extension lectures might copy with advantage. * * *

The following story illustrates one of the few occasions on which the stolid Englishman got the better of the Yankee with a taste for descriptive enlargement: Mr. Charles Francis Adams was show- ing an English friend the chief points of interest in Boston. At Bunker Frill he said, "This is the place where Warren fell." " Oh, indeed, replied the Englishman, ignorant of American history, "was he seriously hurt by his fall ?" " Hurt ?" said Mr. Adams, "he was killed." The Englishman Jooked up at the monument and said," Well, I don't wonder at it—falling so far." * * *

The Primitive Methodists are celebrating their centenary and they may be pardoned for indulging feelings of pride at the remarkable growth of their denomination from extremely small beginnings. They have an interesting history which was reviewed in a sympathetic and able way by Mr. J. Whitley in his lecture at Legh-street on Thursday evening. As one of the oldest members of the circuit Mr. Whitley can speak from experience of the progress of the move- ment in these parts and he has possessed himself of much information about the days when Primitive Methodism was a struggling and almost insignificant Church. His address was a fitting contribution to the celebrations of the centenary and will, we have no doubt, be read with interest by Free Churchmen.

* * The " Heathens " are nothing if not original. In most districts it is required that plans shall conform to the bye-laws but in one instance the village fathers have decided to improve upon this by making the bye- laws conform to the plans. As will be remembered, the tree planters are forbidden to plant upon footpaths of a less width than seven feet whereas the highway regulations only provide for footpaths six feet in width. On Tuesday the members of the Parochial Committee had before them plans for the making of a number of secondary streets and to oblige the tree planters decided that the footpaths should be seven feet. It was pointed out that this involved a breach of the bye-laws and the Committee solved the difficulty by deciding to alter the bye-laws. The Wigton Rural District Council on Tuesday seriously passed a resolution "that we mind our own business." This is a course of procedure which might be copied by local outhorities nearer home. * * * Another instance of commercial candour !—ln the middle of a " winter sale " handbill a tradesman announces:
MEN'S MUFFLERS, JOB LINE. THEY WON'T LAST LONG. This is in the same class with the carpets that "could not be beaten," and the steak puddings "our own smoke."

* * During a heated discussion at the Tunbridge Wells Town Council, one member declared that another was "not fit to clean the boots of the councillors." There were loud cries of " Withdraw," whereupon the speaker retorted, " Very well, I will withdraw ; Mr. -- is fit to clean the boots of the Council !"

* * The "Young British Liberal "in its current issue contains a number of New Year greetings to young British Liberals. The Earl of Crewe writes :—" lam happy to send cordial New Year greetings to the Young British Liberals' Federation. If the Liberal party in Parliament is to fulfil the hopes of those who placed it in power a year ago it must be animated by the qualifies of youth, hope, enthusiasm, and energy." Mr. Winston Churchill wrote :—" All good wishes for the Young British Liberal cause in the year 1907."

div.head: WARRINGTON
div.p: WARRINGTON

Coming Events. Thursday next will be observed by the Beautiful Warrington Society at "tree planting day" when trees will be planted in Church-street. The proceed- ings will commence at 2.30. The programme at the popular penny concert to-nignt, in the Bold-street schools, has been arranged by Mrs. Hubi Newcombe. The artistes will be Miss Marie Houghton, Miss Florence Brown, Miss Dorothy Truslove and Messrs. F. Hartley, J. Forrester, and George Stanley. The annual tea party in connectic‘n with the St. Paul's Church will be held in the Parr Hall on Monday the 28th inst. On the following day the annual dance will be held in the Parr Hall. The Temperance Legislation League are to hold a demonstration in the Parr Hall, on February 4th, at which addresses will he delivered by the Bishop of Liverpool and Mr. H. Vivian M.P, Another effort on behalf of the Infirmary Extension Fund is to be made on Saturday, February 9th, when the members of the Warrington Musical Society will give a miscellaneous concert in aid of that highly deserving object. The programme, which will be provided entirely by members of the Society, is an exceptionally attractive one. The items include several operatic choruses, instrumental selections, and vocal solos. There will be popular prices ranging from 6d. to 3s. The plan will be open at Mr. R. H. Pearson's' 80ld-street, to subscribers on Saturday next and to the general public on the following Wednesday. The annual old boys' dinner in connection with the Boteler Grammar School will be held at the Lion Hotel on Thursday, January 31st. The Rev. Thomas A. Schonberg, M.A., Rector of St. Margaret's, Burnage, Manchester, will preside, and Lord Lilford and the Mayor (Alderman Smethurst) are expected to be present. The annual ball in connection with the Warring- ton Butchers' Association will be held in the Parr Hall on January 31st. Particulars wtll be found in our advertising columns. The Rev. J. F. Matthews resumes his addresses to men in Toft's Assembly Room on Thursday evening next, when the subject of his address will be " The New Theology." A meeting of the Warrington Progressive Labour League will be held at the Liberal Club on Tuesday next, when a debate on "The Unemployed Question," will be introduced by Ur. John Morton. A Liberal demonstration will be held at Stockton Heath on Thursday, January 31st. A meeting to be, held in the Hall Cafe will be addressed, amongst others, by Mr. H. Vivian, M.P., and Mr. Alfred J. King, M.P. Lord Lilford will lay the foundation stone of the Infirmary extension on the 31st inst. He will, after the ceremony, be entertained at a luncheon at the Volunteer headquarters.

Personal. A marriage has been arranged between Mr. George Rolman Kent Kingdon, MA., of Taddyforde House, Exeter, and Stockton Heath, Cheshire, and Katherine Lucy (Kitty) daughter of Mr. W. B. Risk, Paymaster- in-Chief, R.N. (retired), St. Elmo, Weymouth.

PUBLIC BENEFIT'.—UNDER THE CLOCK FOR BEST BOOTS IN LANCASHIRE.—Advt. 1 Shorthand Writers' Association. There was a good attendance at the weekly meeting Ot this Association, held at the Winmarleigh Cafe on , Wednesday night. Speed practice (to which special attention is now being given in view of the spring examinations), was conducted in two sections, at fairly -high and low rates. Miss E. Houghton then read a 'thoroughly enjoyable paper entitled: "How to -succeed as a Typist." In her opening remarks she 'trusted that it would not be considered presumption on her part if she stated that the paper had been vrritlen in the light of practical experience. In referr- jog to a typist's qualifications, the lecturer considered that it was of the utmost importance that such clerks should be possessed of capability and adaptability, and should extend courtesy to all. It was also very ' -essential that enthusiasm be put into one's work, to • 'which should be given full consideration, in order that' iustiee might be done to anytloing that the typist was i called upon to undertake. Miss Houghton urged that i every opportunity be taken of studying commercial subjects—especially languages—so that in due time , the typist might,by her or his own knowledge and zeal,! rise to a more responsible (and, she hoped, lucrative) ' position. The paper war listened to with great atten- Lion.—A vote of thanks to Miss Houghton terminated Lae meeting.

"The Lost Heritage," by Joseph Hatton. Children's Corner. 7. Local Football. Railway Time Table. Warburton Bridge. The Bucklow and Warrington Rural District Councils are in negotiations with the object of arriv- ing at a common basis on which to approach the Manchester Ship Canal Co.,for the abolition of the tolls on Warburton Bridge, which spans the canal and connects Lancashire with Cheshire.

•Death of Miss E. Finney. Much regret will he felt in Latchford and the district at the death of Miss Ethel Blanche Finney, youngest daughter of the late Mr. D. W. Finney, a former respected headmaster of Heathside National School. The deceased lady had been ill for over twelve months suffering from phthisis. The funeral will take place at St. Paul's Church on Monday. Death of Mrs. Ivan Fulton-Smith. We record with deep regret the sudden and unexpected death of Mrs. Ivan Fulton-Smith, which took place at the residence of her parents (Councillor and Mrs. Nield), 18, Salisbury-street, on Sunday. The deceased lady, who had only been married about twelve months, was a daughter-in-law of Councillor Fulton-Smith, and was deeply respected by a large circle of friends,by whom her death is much regretted. Great sympathy has been extended to the bereaved husband and parents, in the sad loss they have sustained.

The Manchester and Liverpool District Bank. A meeting of the shareholders of the Manchester and Liverpool District Banking Company Limited was held on Wednesday, at the Head Office of the Bank in Spring Gardens, Manchester, Mr. Edward Dormer, Chairman of the Bank, presiding. The report of the Directors, recommending a dividend for the half-year of 21s. a share, free from Income Tar, was adopted. At the close of the Shareholders' Meeting the Board of Directors met and re-elected Mr. Edward Donner Chairman, and appointed Mr. Edward Tootal Broadhurst Deputy Chairman. 1

UNDER THE CLOCK for Good BOOTS. Advt.— Death of Mrs. T. Sharrocks. We record with regret the death, which took place at her residence, Grappenhall-road, Stockton Heath, I on Friday, of Mrs. Sharrocks, wife of Mr. T. Sharrocks. I The deceased lady, who was 62 years of age, had been ; ill for some considerable time, death being due to ' cancer. Together with her husband she took a great interest in church affairs and was a regular wor- shipper at St. Thomas's Church. She was widely known and respected and her death is deeply regretted !by a large circle of friends. The funeral took place at St. Thomas's Church on Tuesday, when the service was choral, and was conducted by the Rev. H. V. assisted by the Revs. J. Collins and H. A. Pigott, Lester. The chief mourners were Messrs. T Sharrocks, IW. Gill, G. Gill, A. J. Willett, W. Vincent, F. Rose, IJ. Borthwick, and W. Richardson. Many beautiful ' floral tributes were placed on the grave. Warrington P.S.A. . _

There—was an excellent attendance at the meeting of the above society in the Co-operative Hall, Sankey- street, on Sunday last. The Vice-President (Mr. R. Nelson) presided, and delivered a very interesting address on the "Power of Love." Mr. E. Wynne Jones gave an address on the motto for the year " Let us not be weary in well-doing." Mr. Jones stated that it was our duty to take an interest in every question that affected human life. We must fight against everything that degraded human life, and strive to remove the bad laws, and wicked customs that hindered men living pure lives. We must take our part in the fight of the people for self govern-. ment. We must maintain our freedom and above all we must fight for practical obedience to the universal law of brotherhood.' Councillor Clegg read the Scripture lesson, and prayer was offered by Mr. W. Brown.

General Buller's Visit. Preparations for the visit to Warrington of Sir Redvers Buller, V.C., on February 21st, are being rapidly pushed forward. The committee held a pro- tracted meeting at the Town Hall yesterday afternoon and many suggestions were discussed. The final arrangements will, however, depend upon the time at the disposal of the distinguished visitor. It is hoped that it will be possible for the unveiling of the memorial in Queen's Gardens to take place at about three o'clock in the afternoon, in order that the townspeople may have an opportunity of witnessing it. The General will be met at the station by a guard of honour and escorted to the Town Hall where he will be received by the Mayor and the Chairman and members of the Execu- tive Committee. Afterwards the party will probeed to the Queen's Gardens for the ceremony of the day and on its conclusion a luncheon will be given in the Parr Hall.

Handball. At the Borough Gymnasium, Palmyra Square, on Wednesday before a moderate attendance, Warrington fulfilled their League fixture with Liverpool, Myrtle St. Gymnasium, Mr. J. Kinsley,Gymnasium instructor, officiating as referee. Warrington threw off, and Holloway for the home team, almost secured a goal from long range, the ball falling on the side of the basket. Some very interesting play followed, the tackling on both sides being keen and vigorous, but without any fouls. After several unsuccessful attempts at goal, Bibby secured the first goal for the home team. The Liverpool backs played a quick game, but the forwards did not seem to have much chance of scoring, their shots being erratic, through the keen tackling of the home backs. Warrington had hard lines in not registering two or three more goals in the-. second half,the forwards receiving good passes from the backs. Regan registered the 2nd goal with a good shot for the home team, and the game finished with Warrington 2 goals, Liverpool 0.. Death of Mr. William Horton. The death took place at his residence, Wilderspool- causeway, on Monday, of Mr. William Horton. The deceased gentleman, who was 48 years of age, had been a director of Henry Milling and Co. for about 25 years. Mr. Horton, who was much respected, was at the shop no later than Wednesday last. He bad been ailing for some time, but his death was quite unexpected. He leaves a widow and three children. I The funeral took place at Lymm Parish Church, on Thursday and Was the occasion of a striking demon.- , stratidn of respect. The service was conducted by , the Rev. G. B. Thurston. Thil cortege from Lymm station was preceeded by Messrs. Milling's staff and the chief mourners were : Mr. P. Horton (son), Mr.l J. H. Horton and Mr. T. Horton (brothers), Mr. F. Warburton and Mr. J. Hall (brothers-in-law). Messrs. ; H. Milling and Co., were represented by Messrs. H. Milling, T. .A Milling, J. Walton, Robert Lowe I and amongst others present were Mr. W. Leigh ; and Mr. Fairclough and Mr. Davidson (Man- chester). Amongst the wreaths which were 'placed on the grave were those from the directors of H. Milling and 00., Messrs. Milling's staff and thel Warrington and District Grocers' and Provision Dealers' Association.

" Dr. Wake's Patient " at Parr Hall. Next week promises to be a very busy week for the Warrington Dramatic Society who are advertised to give five performances of the highly successful comedy "Dr. Wake's Patient," in Parr Hall. This charming comedy is well known to local theatre goers as it will be remembered it was played by an excellent company only a few months ago in the Royal Court Theatre. The local cast it a very strong one con- taining many ladies and gentleman who have on several occasions proved themselves to possess histrionic abilities of a very high order. We understand the play has been well rehearsed and that the high standard of the Society's previous productions will be fully maintained. A full dress rehearsal on the stage has been fixed for Monday evening. The first publio performance will be given on Tuesday evening and repeated each evening during the week. As on previous occasions charity will benefit by the performances, the proceeds this year being given to the Infirmary Extension Fund. It must be very gratifying to the Society that as the result of their various efforts, extending over a long period of years, over £2,00 bass been raised for local charities and it is to be hoped this sum will be con- siderably increased as the result of next week's work. The plan of dress and reserved seats can be seen at Mr. H. Ashton's, Sankey-street, and seats can still be booked for each performance.
