div.head: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
div.p: EARLESTOWN AND NEWTON
GAS WORKERS' ANNUAL SUPPER.

Thefifth annual supper of the _Newton Urban District Council gas workers was held on Saturday at the Oak Tree Hotel, Newton-le-Willows. About 35 sat down to supper, after which a very good programme was gone through, and a most enjoyable evening spent. -Mr. A. Bowes (engineer) took the chair, and Mr. J. T. Hoggard (manager) the vice-chair. An interesting musical programme was gone through, and several toasts were submitted and well-received. '..••••••

div.head: LECTURE AT THE TOWN HALL.
div.p: LECTURE AT THE TOWN HALL.

A lecture was given at the Town Hall on Monday by Mr. William Stirling, M.D., LL.D., D.Sc., professor of physiology in the Victoria University of Manchester, on " The daily wear and tear of the body." It was illustrated by lantern slides and experiments. Mr. C. B. F. Borron presided. The hall was crowded, and a very interesting lecture was delivered, which was thoroughly enjoyed.

div.head: THEFT FROM A HOTEL.
div.p: THEFT FROM A HOTEL.

John Mitchell, of Earlestown, was charged at the Occasional Court on Monday with stealing from the bar of the Swan Hotel, Newton Common, Earlestown, on the 12th inst., an electric box and contents, value £3 belonging to Mr. J. Naylor. Prisoner was seen to abstract the box from behind the bar and go into the yard. Inforination was given to the police and prisoner was arrested by P.C. Simpson. He was remanded to the Warringtln County Petty Sessions where on Wednesday he was sent to gaol for a month.

div.head: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. N. SIDDELEY.
div.p: SUDDEN DEATH OF MR. N. SIDDELEY.

We regret to hear of the sudden death of Mr. N. Siddeley, which took place at his residence, Ilighbury, Wargrave, Earlestown. The deceased gentleman was apparently well when he retired to rest, but early on Tuesday morning he seemed to be suffering from a seizure of some kind. Medical aid was called in, but his recovery seemed doubtful and he died later in the day from heart failure. Mr. Siddely had represented the Viaduct Ward for about 13 years, and was highly respected in the district. Mach sympathy is felt for the widow, who has been in indifferent health for some time.

div.head: TRADESNIAN'S EXTRAORDINARY WILL.
div.p: TRADESNIAN'S EXTRAORDINARY WILL.

' An application arising out of an extraordinary will made by the late Mr. Benjamin Walker, of 6outhport, and for many years the proprietor of a shop at Earles- town, and a great friend of the Wesleyans, was heard in the Probate Court on Monday by Mr. Justice Bargrave Deane. It appeared that the deceased gentleman died in November last,leaving estate valued at £58,000 and a holograph will dated 18th September, 1906. A curious feature, said counsel, was that a piece of stamp paper had been stuck over words which affected the disposi- tion of about £3,000. One of the questions was whether this piece of stamp paper could be removed or whether it constituted an obliteration, and the words underneath coull be read.—Mr. Middleton, who appeared for certain charities concerned, submitted that the matter could not be properly disposed by application.— Mr. Justice Bargrave Deane thought it could not be done without a general consent. The proper way would be to bring a Probate action.—Mr. Bayford, who appeared for the executors, said his clients had no objection to bringing an action, and the matter stood over.

div.head: DISASTROUS FIRE AT EARLESTOWN
div.p: DISASTROUS FIRE AT EARLESTOWN
Great Damage at the Vulcan Foundry.

One of the most disastrous fires which has ever occurred at Earlestown broke out in the early hours of Tuesday morning at the Vulcan L oundry Company's locomotive engineering works,one of the most important industrial concerns of its kind in Lancashire.

It appears that as the night watchman was going his rounds between twelve and one o'clock he visited part of the works known as the "old turning shop." In this particular department the men left off at eight o'clock on Monday evening for the day. The forge, which is some distance away, however, was in full work at the time. The watchman discovered an outbreak of fire in one corner, and at once gave an alarm to the employees in the forge. Messengers were at once despatched for the local fire brigade, who received notification about half-past one and although over a mile away from the works reached there in quick time under Superintendent Haggard. The London and North-Western Brigade from the Viaduct Waggon Works with their manual engine, followed directly after. The brigade were hampered in dealing at the outset with the fiercely-burning premises through shortness of water, and the machinery in the intervening shops proving great obstacles to thl3 men handling the hose. It was half-past two before there was anything like an adequate supply of water being turned on to the premises. Jets from the water mains were meanwhile being directed on the adjoining buildings, which frequently became ignited. These included a very elaborate electrical installation, pattern makers, joiners and packing shops, and boiler foundry on an extensive scale. The roof of the old building, however, fell in in sections, bringing with it rafte..s, shafting' and pulley, which sent up millions of sparks and lurid tongues of flame, which all the while threatened to involve the other premises. But the brigades succeeded in prevent- ing the area of the conflagration extending, and by four o'clock were distinctly gaining a mastery. Messrs. M'Corquodale and Co.'s fire engine was quickly on the scene. The men devoted themselves to the seeing of the dynamo-house, and worked very successfully, their purpose being effected. The Warrington, Leigh, and St. Helens Corporation brigades had been telegraphed for, and they arrived about four o'clock with their steam fire engines. The four brigades concentrated their efforts with great effect, and not only saved the surrounding premises, but quenched the flames very quickly in the gutted turning shop. Quite recently the destroyed premises were equipped with new machinery of great diversity of character to meet the demands made upon the capacity of the works whose owners have in hand many large orders for loco- motives for the Argentine and Indian State railways, and upon which the men were working overtime. Over a thousand men are employed in the various shops. Two hundred or more found work in the department which has been destroyed. The fire will probably not affect the boiler-making shop and forge. The amount of damage has not been computed, but it must reach £20.000.

The disaster is a most unfortunate one, as the Vulcan Foundry is the only place that has been working full time in Earlestown recently. Only a little while ago trade was depressed by the closing up of an extensive paper-making mill in the neighbourhood, and other works have not been brisk.

The work of clearing away the debris from the machine shop was proceeded with before noon, and it was later stated that the works would be opened as usual, the men employed in the part of the works affected by the fire being found employment in other shops. An examination of the machine revealed the fact that this had not suffered as heavily as was antici- pated, the majority of the 'machines being practically in good working order. Great credit is due to the brigades engaged in the by no means easy task of extinguishing.the flames, great pluck and tact being displayed from first to last. The Warrington Fire Brigade returned to Warrington shortly before noon on Tuesday.

div.head: CELEBRATIONS AT LECH STREET CHURCH.
div.p: CELEBRATIONS AT LECH STREET CHURCH.
Interesting Lecture by Mr. J. Whitley.

The present year is one of great interest in the history of the Primitive Methodist Church. marking as it does the centenary of the denomination. Naturally the occasion is being celebrated with great enthusiasm, for the record of the Church during its one hundred years' existence is one of remarkable progress. The commemoration at Legh-street Church, Warrington, is taking the form of special services which were inaugurated on Thursday evening and will be continued during the coming week. The feature of Thursday's gathering was an interesting lecture by Mr. J. Whitley, of Stockton Heath, on Lie history of Primitive Methodism. The Rev. C. L. Stowe presided over a fair attendance.

Mr. WHITLEY said he fully realized that it was by the unanimous desire of the Circuit officials that he, as being the oldest official in the station, should undertake that first and most important part in the Connexional 'Centenary services at Warrington and he therefore with I gratitude and thankfulness most readily complied with the request. The year 1907 was his jubilee year as a member of the connexion, having joined in membership with the Primitive Methodists on the 24th February, 1857, and having remained a member ever since. He very highly prized the first class tickets, which he now held, given to him in that year by the Rev. Thomas Kench who then travelled in the circuit of which Warrington formed Dart. Passing on to the subject of the lecture, Mr, Whitley said that in 1807 their Church began in much obscurity, but the commencement of the present century found them as a Church standing the fourth in strength and influence for good among the Evangelical Free Churches of England and,with only one exception, the largest of the Methodist Churches. Truly this led them to say" God hath done great things for us whereof we are glad." Very early in the last century that most remarkable and distinguished personage Lorenzo Dow came over from America. He was distinguished for holding open- air religious services, and had been moved to cross the Atlantic and speak in England. He came over in the little ship" Centurion" which belonged to a Quaker, and the only woman on the vessel was his wife Peggy. Leaving New York on November 10th, 1805, the journey occupied 37 days, their quick arrival being attributed to favourable weather and fair winds. Lorenzo was indeed a most striking figure; pale and sallow in complexion, his face deeply marked with small-pox. His hair was allowed to grow until it reached his waist and a pair of eyes of unnatural brightness peered out,between his flowing locks. He held his hearers spell-bound by his eloquence, which was of the Qaaker Methodist type. After preaching in Liverpool and , Warrington some time, and here making his stay in the humble and hospitable home of Peter Phillips to whom he became greatly attached, be journeyed into Stafford- shire where he became acquainted with Hugh and James Bourne. After several conversations and much prayer, they arranged to hold a camp meeting, and on the 31st May 1807, that

FIRST AND MOST MEMORABLE MEETING was held on Mow Cop, on the borders of Cheshire and Staffordshire. It commenced about six o'clock in the morning and continued until about 8 in the evening and during these hours there was continnal prayer and preaching, thousands of persons attending. These camp meetings and other open air services were held frequently afterwards. It was an interesting recollec- tion to him (Mr. Whitley) that on May 31st 1885 he had the privilege of preaching on Mow Cop at a camp meeting. Continuing the history, the lecturer said that at the first open air services ten persona—Joseph and Mary Slater, Elizabeth Baker, Susannah and Sarah Rowcroft, Ralph and Mary Goodwin, Samuel Simcox, Thomas Redfern and Isaac tielford—were converted,and being prevented from joining in membership with any other church, formed themselves into a class and their first meeting was held on March 14th; 1810. This was the foundation of the Primitive Methodist Connexion Bournes and Clowes afterwards joined the new church thus formed, H. liourne's name being left off the Wesleyan plan and William Clowes being expelled from that body in June 1810. It should be noted, however, that the class which formed the nucleus of the Primitive Methodist Connexion, consisted of new converts who were not connected with any church, and therefore it was not a division or split from any other body, but entirely a new Church, raised up by God to accomplish great good for Him. After this feeble and small beginning plans were printed regularly, the first being dated 1812, March, April, May and June, and at the meeting called to make this plan, the denominational name was chosen—Primitive Metho- dist. There were 33 places for preaching and 21 preachers on this plan, W. Clowes and James Crawford as travelling preachers receiving 10s. per week each for preaching anywhere they saw fit. There were 19 local preachers an their appointments were sometimes from 30 to 50 miles away, which distance they had to walk. They preached and formed churches at villages through which they passed, the places named being in Stafford- shire, Derbyshire, Lancashire and Cheshire.

div.head: PROGRESS AND SUCCESS.
div.p: PROGRESS AND SUCCESS.

These remarkable men began to preach the Gospel in the open air from village to village, town to town, and city to city, on the village greens, in the busy market places, in fact everywhere. Clowes from Burslern, and Crawford from Delamere Forest were remarkably successful in the salvation of thousands of souls. The church which began with ten members had, on the com- pletion of the.century,a membership of over 200,000, not counting the tens of thousands it had been the means of landing safe in the heaven of eternal repose and happiness. What had made Primitive Methodism the power it was? To his mind it was to be attributed under Almighty!God to the sanctified, self- sacrificing, zealous, thoroughly consecrated and laborious efforts of their forefathers in the Connexion. Mr. Whitley then referred briefly to the lives and work of William Clowes, Thomas Russell and William Garner. He pointed out that Clowessacrificedan income from his trade of £2 to £3 a week in order to become a preacher for the pay of 10s. a week. He endured terrible hard- ships and travelled almost incredible distances on foot to preach the gospel. He said that at some place in the neighbourhood of Warrington in 1811 he met with very indifferent treatment. At one place the people threw water at him while preaching and created much disturbance. "On my way back to Warrington, a distance of seven Miles "he said" I was waylaid. The rebels rushed upon rile suddenly and threw stones and clods of dirt, but I shouted to God for help and He helped me and confounded my persecutors. I preached several times at Warrington after this and had great success." Mr. Whitley de- tailed some of the long journeys undertaken by Clowes and also spoke of the work of Hugh Bourne who took the largest share in the management of the Connexion and before his death visited America. Some striking figures were quoted showing the remarkable progress of the church before Clowes' death in 18s1, the membership having been raised to 104,702 while there were 103,310 scholars and 1,355 chapels. The success- fut efforts of two converts—T. Russell and W. Garner— were next noticed and the persecutions which they under- went were described. In one instance Russell walked 130 miles in five days, preaching and exhorting on the way. He was once taken into custody for preaching and committed for three months as a vagrant. William Garner in speaking of the labours of Russell and himself said that" in twenty-one years I have travelled on foot with comparatively trifling exceptions 44,93 t miles and have preached 6,278 sermoas and these do not include exhortations, addresses, missionary speeches, &c., which amounted to a great number." In 'conclusion Mr. Whitley said a spiritually working active ' ministry and Church, harmoniously combined, must be successful and a power in the world in seeking out, enlightening and elevating t' a higher level the poor and down-trodden and bringing them to Christ. Wide were the fields of usefulness open to them as a denomi- nation and Church to-day, arid tremendous and solemn were the responsibilities resting upon them. But he had

div.head: FAITH IN THE FUTURE,
div.p: FAITH IN THE FUTURE,

for everything was favourable to them. The signs of the times and their churches in many places were bright with hope. They lived in an age of progress and advancement, and their appliances and means were greater and better than ever. Educativn and training better fitted them for their work ; their journeys were shorter, their places of worship mom numerous and larger, their hearers more ready and willing to receive them. They lived in new times and seen many changes, but with faith in God he believed their work would prosper. (Applause). The Rev. C. L. STovve, in expressing the thanks of the meeting to Mr. Whitley, said he thought the success of Primitive Methodism was to be found hi its evangelism or revivalism and also in its democratic character. They had always been a Church of the people, many of their ministers being -recruited from the working- classes. They also owed a great deal to their definite church organization, and to their circuit system, and to the prominent part they had taken in temperance work. Their • care for the children had been an outstanding feature and it could be said that they had moved with the times and were not a stereotyped church.
Mr. GRIFFITHS IliSO spoke of the democratic character of the Primitive Methodist Church and 'pointed out that not a few Labour Al.P.'s were members of the denomination.

Next week's meetings will be addressed as follows: Monday, "Our Origin and History," Mr. T. B. Parkes; Tuesday, "Our Founders," Mr. %V. Higginson ; Wednes- day (at Knutsford-road) "Our Institutions," Mr. J. Griffiths: Thursday, "Our Missions," Mr. H. Billing- ham ; Friday." Our Aims." Mr. H. S. Atkin ; Saturday, "Our Great Need," Mr. E. Cooper.

The committee which arranged a carnival ball at Grasengruen, in Austria, charged for entrance tickets according to the weight of the visitors. Sixpence per stone was the rate fixed, and a weighing machine was set up at the entrance.

div.head: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
div.p: RUNCORN AND WIDNES.
A CARNEGIE OFFER TO RUNCORN.
Mr. Andrew Carnegie has promised to give .E3lO towards the purchase of a new organ to lioly Trinity Church, Runcorn, on condition that an instrument of not less value than £7OO is obtained.
ALLEGED SILVER THEFTS AT WIDNES.

At Widnes, on Monday morning, Michael Riley, Esther-street, and Joseph Carrol, Albert-road, appeared before the bench on remand charged with stealing Sibs. 10oz. of metallic silver, value £2l, the property of Messrs. Dennis and Company, copper smelters, Widnes. The case was again remanded and Riley was released on his usual £5O and two £25, and Carrol himself in .C2O ' and two in £5.

div.head: ACCIDENT AT WIDNES WORKS.
div.p: ACCIDENT AT WIDNES WORKS.

I A man named John Reed, aged thirty-six, hailing from county Mayo, Ireland, was admittQd to the Accident Hospital, Widnes, at noon on Tuesday, suffer- ing from a badly lacerated wound on the lag and other 1 bruises. Reed had managed to gain admittance to Maspratt's works, and though evidently looking for a ,fa he spoke to no one. As a locomotive, which had shunted some waggons into a sliding, was passing him, by some means he fell under the engine, which was, fortunately, only travelling at a walking pace. The driver, seeing the man's predicament, quickly reversed the engine, and saved him from more serious injury. SIR J. T. BRUNNER AND MAGISTERIAL APPOINTMENTS.

Sir J. T. Brunner, 1N1.P., in a letter regarding the appointment of magistrates and Lord Loreburn's remarks on the point, says that the proper course now is that he should call the committee together a day or , two after the opening of next session, to take the Lord Chancellor's letter into consideration and to report to another meeting of Liberal and Labour members. The matter may safely and properly be left in the hands of the general body, which is the only dignified course. ALKALI. WORKS INSPECTION.

The appointment of a new inspector for the Widnes and Runcorn districts, under the Alkali Works Regula- tion Act, by the combined authorities of South-west Lancashire and Cheshire, has called attention to the necessity for increased supervision. The Liverpool Corporation have expressed the desire that an additional inspector should be appointed, and that the basis of contribution by the respective authorities should be the area and not the rateable value of the district. A con- ference of representatives has been held in Liverpool, and the Much Woolton District Council has expressed its willingness to contribute fifty per cent. more on the present basis of contribution, and suggested that the other districts surrounding Widnes and Runcorn be approached with the view of inducing them to contribute a proportion of the salary of the additional inspector on the same basis.

• THEFT OF METAL AT WIDNES. At the Widnes Police Court on Monday morning, Peter Grady was charged with stealing 741 b. of lead,the property of the Widnes Alkali Company, on a date between the Bth and 12th inst. At six on Saturday morning Police-Sergeant Davidson and Police-Constable Jones secreted themselves in an entry near Travis-street • and after waiting some time they saw Grady enter M'Conville's marine store yard with something bulky under his coat. It was afterwards identified as belong- • ing to the Alkali Company. Prisoner pleaded guilty to the charge. Search was afterwards made at his home and another quantity was found under the bed. Michael M'Conville was also charged with stealing 291 b. of lead, the property of the United Alkali Company. He was further charged with receiving lead, well knowing it to , have been stolen. Search of prisoner's stable revealed a bag of lead weighing 91b.—Superintendent Strickland asked for a remand,and this was granted,only M'Conville ' being allowed bail himself in £lO and two sureties of £lO each.

div.head: PITIFUL TRAGEDY AT WIDNES.
div.p: PITIFUL TRAGEDY AT WIDNES.
FATHER BURNT TO DEATH AND SON

DROWNED. On Friday last Thomas Hankinson, aged Cl years, a labourer, of 74, Pear-street, met with a tragic death. The deceased was employed at the Widnes Foundry, and a portion of his duties was to light some gas jets which were situated in a huge oven used for drying moulds. At eleven o'clock, Joseph Gilhooly went to the oven, where a horrible sight met his gaze. Hankin- son had fallen, probably in a fit, or from the effects of the gas, on to the jets, which became ignited, and he was so badly burnt about the head, face, and hands, that life was extinct.—There is yet another calamity for the sorrowful family. At three o'clock on Sunday afternoon. Frederick Samuel Hankinson, aged seven years, son of the above, was playing on the canal bank ,near to the Iron Bridge. He fell in and was drowned in the presence of his sister. The body was recovered by an engine-driver named Daintith, and was conveyed to the hospital. Mr. Brighouse held the inquest on Thomas Hankinson at the Accident Hospital, Widnes, on Tuesday. Joseph Gilhooley. a labourer, said he went into the stove at eleven o'clock on Friday morning to adjust a jet, and. found the deceased tying on the floor with his face resting on one of the jets.—Dr. Lindsay said that in company with Dr. Brebner he had made a post-mortem examination. He found a clot of blood on the brain and the left lung was destroyed. His opinion was that Hankinson died from natural causes. Heart failure had been accelerated by the condition of the left lung It was possible that the amount of carbonic oxide gas inthe stove had a tendency to throw a strain on the heart and lungs which they could not sustain.—Mr. Knowles (for the company) said that that was only a possibility.—After a private conference with the jury the Coroner decided to adjourn the inquest in order that the jury might examine the stove.—Another inquest was held, upon Frederick Samuel Hankinson, aged seven, son of the deceased man Thomas Hankinson, who was drowned near the iron bridge, Widnes. on Sunday, in the Sankey and St. Helens Canal. His sister stated that they went for a walk, and when near the bridge he fell in. The body was afterwards recovered by an engine driver named Daintith. The jury returned a verdict of 'Accidental death."

div.head: ST. HELENS.
div.p: ST. HELENS.
CHARGE AGAINST A PHOTOGRAPHER.

William H. Greenway, a photographer, of Leeds, was charged at St. Helens on Saturday with stealing a camera and embezzling Ll us. lid, the money of W. H. Campbell, photographer, of Duke-street. Prisoner was brought by a couple of warders from Wakefield Prison, where he is undergoing imprisonment. The Chief Constable told the magistrates that the prisoner was wanted by a large number of police forces for thefts of a similar kind. On November 18.1905, this man applied for work to Mr. Campbell, and was given it. He worked one week, and then decamped with the camera and money he had drawn for photographs. It appeared that he went to Stockport and sold the camera and defrauded the two parties out of the money. Last month he was tried at the Leeds Assizes and sent to g3ol. The magistrates committed Greenway for trial at the Liverpool Quarter Sessions on Tuesday. Greenway appeared at the Liverpool Sessions on Tuesday and pleaded guilty. Mr. Greaves Lord, who prosecuted, stated that there were a great number of charges against Greenway, who was wanted by the police in different parts of the country. For a long time he had been systematically defrauding photo- graphers. A sentence of six months imprisonment with hard labour was passed. ST. HELENS CONGREGATIONAL MEN'S BIBLE

div.head: CLASS.
div.p: CLASS.

Colonel W. W. Pilkington on Sunday afternoon pre- sided at a special service commemorating the eighth anniversary of the St. Helens Congregational Men's Bible Class. There was a very large congregation. Mr. Harry Berrey's St. Helens Prize Choir rendered several choruses in grand style, notably Mendelssohn's "Thanks be to God" and Sullivan's "0, gladsome light." The Chairman congratulated the officials of the class on its success. During the year the mernber§hip had increased very considerably, and was now 310. He hoped it, would go on developing, for he felt it was a clahs which all the men connected with the Congrega- tional churches ought to support. A social club had been started in connection witd the class, and it was in a very satisfaCtory state. —The Rev. J. H. Robinson, of Burnley, who had taken the place of the Rev. Fred Hibbert, of Blackburn, gave an interesting address. A. collection was takeu for the class benevolent fund. POETRY AND IMPOSTURE. George Reynolds, of Liverpool, was charged at St Helens, on Saturday, with obtaining charitable contri- butions by fraud. Reynolds was arrested by Police Constable Smirthwaite when he was distributing printed forms headed "The appeal of the unemployed.' On the forms there were a number of verses with an appeal.— The, Chief Constable said this man and several otllers had introduced a system of silent begging. Three gangs had visited St. Helens, and they were all impostors. Although this man pretended to be a decent workman, he had not worked for years, and he had been convicted for highway robbery with violence at Liverpool, and for a similar offence at Wigan and Runcorn. He had been granted a pedlar's certificate by the Barrow-in-Furness police.—Reynolds was sent to gaol for three months, and said when leaving the dock, You will have a case of murder when I come out."

div.head: SOCIALISM.
div.p: SOCIALISM.
MR. E. OSBORNE AND THE:. JUNIOR LIBERALS.
Interesting Discussion.

There was a crowded attendance,at the meeting of the Warrington Junior Liberal Association on Monday when a paper on " Why I am a Socialist " was delivered by Mr. E. Osborne, an ex-president of the Association. The meeting was held at Gregory's Cafe, Mr. J. Hawthorne presiding. Mr. OSBORNE, said that since he hold the office of President of the Association many things had happened. He felt that he could no longer remain president, and it had been deemed advisable for the society to become ' affiliated with the Young British Liberals' Association. He was no longer a Liberal; that, he supposed, meant that he, or the Liberal Party, had changed. There were some persons who prided themselves on the lact that they tiad held the same views from their youth up. They placed themselves in an awkward dilemma, inas- much as they either knew all that was to be known when then they were young or else they had been slow and had stood just where they were. There were others who suffered from a certain docility of mind who made a few inquiries and were easily satisfied with what they were told. Study to them was a bore. Generally speaking, however, people changed in bulk as the exigeecies of party tactics demanded them to do. He (the speaker) was a Socialist, and official Liberalism was opposed to Socialism, and for proof of that assertion he directed attention to the remit utterances of several Liberal leaders. He dis- claimed all connection with the fairy stories many had heard concerning Socialism, which did not mean "robbing the rich to give to the poor." Neither did it mean robbing the poor to make the rich richer. It did not intend to take all the money, place it in a huge pile and then" share and share alike." Neither did it intend that a few should continue to share it amongst them- selves. It would not "equalize men's fortunes and men's positions," as Mr. Asquith believed; but it would insist upon equality of opportunity. and an absence of extreme wealth oia the one hand and starvation and abject misery on the other. (Applause.) It would not make Atheists of them all. It would make it easier, however, for a man to practice what he preached, to make business methods less dirty, to have less need for Nypocrisy in the daily businese routine, and the camel would have a better chance of getting through the needle's eye. He would ask them not to confound Socialism with trade unionism and the co-operative movement. In many ways they were excellent institutions, but they were net Socialism. They must not think of it as anarchism, as agnosticism, as atheism, as body-snatching, and a number of other imaginings to which the opponents of Socialism had ascribed importance.

lequitably distributed • :=-: Was- every man to receive a. reward according to his contribution to the joint stock or according to his need? Mr. Osborne said the rail- ways, &c., should be purchased. It seemed to him that every thorough-going Socialist would sweep away that capital altogether, because the purchase would simply mean the transmission of the payment to another source. He was in favour of a great deal of what Mr. Osborne • said. He always had been and always would be in favour of land nationalization, but he maintained that a' man should have the reward of his labour, the whole reward and nothing but the reward. (Applause). Mr. HAMPSON, of the Independent Labour Party, said . he was surprised at the Chairman's remarks in regard to municipal and state undertakings. It must be recog- nized that municipalities were governed by men of the capitalist class, but it could not be said that the tram- way workers in Liverpool were not better off than the' employees in the days of prirate•enterprise.With regard to Mr. Parker's question, a man would receive accord- ing to his need. A man with six children would receive' enough to keep six children, and a man with twelve would receive enough to keep them. kHear, hear). Councillor BALL said that under Socialism every man would receive according to his ne:d. It had been proved that there was sufficient in the store house of nature to supply every man, woman and child and if there were people ill fed, ill' clothed it was not because of the lack of material but because of the inequality of the diatribution of wealth. In reference to the purchase of the railways &a. They recognized that a sudden changewould be cruel but they would not allow the payments to continue indefinitely.. So long as a man lived he would have his interest but when life ended his interest disappeared. (Applause). Mr. H. W. GUEST thought the Socialistic ideal would only be brought about by a change in human nature and not by a change in conditions and he failed to see how the Christian spirit which was necessary was to be brought about by state socialism. (Rear, hear). The Rev. H. DUNNICO said he thought every man should receive what he contributed to the state. Under the present system that was impossible because there were social wrecks who had to be kept. Under Socialism those wrecks would disappear and every man would be able to contribute value to the state. (Hear, hear). Mr. HALEY asked whether the Junior Liberal Association were in favour of the present capitalist system?

-Mr. BARNES was proceeding to criticise Mr. Osborne's paper when a little breeze arose. He was referring to a letter which Mr. Osborne wrote to the Press when that gentleman rose and vigorously protested against the introduction of personalities. Peace was restored and Mr. Barnes resumed.
A brief reply by nr.Osborne brought the proceedings to a close.

div.head: WHAT SOCIALISNI MEANS.
div.p: WHAT SOCIALISNI MEANS.

To show what the principles were he would refer to the objects of two recognised Socialist parties—the Fabian Society and the Independent Labour Party. The Fabian Society aimed at the reorganisation of society by the emancipation of land and capital from individual and claes ownership and the vestinc, of them in the communiiy for the general benefft. 'ln that way only could the natural and acquired advantages of the country be equitably shared by all. The object of the Indepen- dent Labour Party was an industrial commonwealth founded upon the socialism of land and capital. The land being the storehouse of all the necessaries of life should be declared and treated as public property; the capital necessary for individual opera- tions should be owned and used collectively; work and wealth resulting therefrom should be 'equitably distributed over the population. He hoped they would not confound the word equity with equaiity.Equity meant right as founded on the laws of nature: fairness and justice. All Socialists agreed that land and indus- trial capital should be the common property of the democracy, and should be used and governed by the people and for the people. In other words what the people collectively needed that they should collectively hold and use. Many people were concerned at the rapid growth of municipalization. The towns owned under- takings some Of which were profitable and some other- wise, yet all were equally necessary. Why should all the non-profitable undertakings be managed by' the people and only some of the profitable ; and why was it necessary to municipalize any of the undertakings instead of continuing along the lines of old-fashioned administration? Did they not see that a gradual evolution had been going on in domestic and industrial affairs, and that by slow degrees the people were acquiring what was theirs by natural right—a voice in the management of their own affairs. The King's highway was no longer maintained merely for convenience of the Royal armies but was now used for the convenience of public traffic. So Socialists said tbat having municipalized the paving, sewerage, lighting &c., the question of municipalizing the houses, clothing, bread and all the necessaries of life was simply a matter of time. If they were prepared to admit that the undertakings which had already been municipalized had been beneficial to the community it surely could not be absurd to suppose that further extension of municipal ownership would prove equally beneficial. In fact whilst people were crying out against Socialism, chiefly because they did not understand it, they were, unconsciously voting for its development every day of their lives. The only arguments he had heard against the further extension of municipal undertakings were not objections to municipalization, but to the fact that it would lead to jobbery and municipal scandals. They knew that cause must precede effect. Therefore if they removed the cause they removed the effect at the same time. Municipal corruption was caused by the desire for private gain and was due not to excess of municipal Socialism but to excess of private enterprise. If they stopped the necessity for private gain they would stop corruption. Accordingly the more Socialism they got and the less need for fear of corruption. Seeing that it was impossible for a man, especially if he lived in a -town, to provide most of the eguisites of life himself, was it not better that the municipality should provide 'them for him? Adulteration would be reduced to a minimum and the profits would be used for-the benefits of all and not of a few. STATE OWNERSHIP. The State owned the post office, tele&raphs, dock- yards, telephones, &c., why therefore, Raid it not acquire the railways, canals, land and factories? There was no need for him to have to prove that railway- systems could be worked more cheaply and more effici- ently under State control than by private enterprise. In continental countries where the railways were owned $y the State the rates of carriage were much lower than in Eagland and yet in spite of this, in Belgium, where the rates were lowest, the railways earned a handsome profit. Dealing with industries Mr. Osborne mentioned a company which since 1892 had paid dividends ranging from 100 per cent to 35 per cent. Those profits made by those workers went to swell capital already accumu- lated in the hands of others. That capital would then. doubtless be employed to create further capital and would thus become a further tribute to industry and lidleness. Mr. Osborne proceeded to illustrate the handi- cap upon industry by reason of mining royalties and rents. Sir Henry Campbell Bannerman said " we wish to make the land less of a pleasure ground for the rich, and more of a treasure house for the nation," and socialists contended that that could only be brought about by the nation owing the land. Many might agree with that but their difficulty would be as to how the land, railw iys and canals were to be acquired. He would reply in exactly the same manner as the tele- phone had been acquired—by purchase." Some were opposed to Socialism because they believed that the handing over of the conduct of industry to the State was opposed to the principle of industrial liberty. Unfortunately for them the State already owned and managed some of the industries. He had heard people object to Socialism on the ground that there tvould be a great tendency for the slow man to set the pace ; that there would be no poetry, no art, no literature- in fact no anything, because there would be no incentive. Poetry, art and literature were however, not menials of the money mania. Artists might be compelled to sell their work but all the money, in the mint could not purchase their temperament and skill. Socialism was more than an economic change —it represented the true form of government. Life was to be made worth living. Men and women were to be enabled to become nobler; political actions were to become sincere; ideals were not to be stifled by selfish- ness ; children were not to be brought into existence to be reared in drudgery and then•to eke out a living by inhuman and degrading self-sacrifice to man-made gods; man was to be respected for his manhood and not for his smartness in amassing we:llth whilst so many millions of his fellow-beings were living on the verge of starvation. (Applause). In opening the discussion which followed the reading of the paper, Mr. HA.WTHORNE said the principles of Liberalism were so broad that Mr. Osborne might have remained a member of the party and still held his socialistic opinions. Mr. Osborne had mentioned a nnmber of socialistic institutions or State controlled industries but who had brought that about? As a matter of fact many of the things to which the lecturer had referred were in operation long before the Independent Labour Party was thought of. In the event of the socialization of all industries he doubted whether the worker was going to be in such an ideal state as Mr. Osborne had depicted. Was it not true that in the postal service the employees were seething with discontent. In regard to the purchase of the railways it would in effect be merely the trans- ferring of the capital to bondholders to whom interest would have to be paid and that interest would have to come out of the workers. (Hear, hear.) Mr. C. E. PARKER asked if, under Socialism, every man would get the product of his labour or if that principle would be altogether transformed. He would like something more definite on the point. He was afraid many Socialists would not own Mr. Osborne. He had only gone half-way and would have to go a great deal further or else retract altogether. The general idea was that every man under Socialism would give according to his abibity And receive according to his need.- Was that the princiNe Mr. Osborne would go upon when he said everything should be

On Monday evening the members of the St. Peter's Church mothers' meeting held their annual tea in . the schoolroom, when about 120 mothers and friends attended. Games and music followed a substantial tea and songs were rendered by Nits. Yeomans and Master. Jack Greaves.One hundred and thirty articles of clothing were distributed among the mothers, having been kindly given by Lady Greenall, Miss Comber, and the Warring- - ton and South Lancashire Needlework Guilds. Each mother on leaving received a mince pie. On Tuesday about 125 of the members of the Young Women's Bible Class and friends spent a most enjoyable evening. Refreshments were served, and the Vicar complimented the girls on their regular ateudance, and said they had an excellent example set them by their teacher, Mrs.. Percival.

On Sunday morning the Rev. John Gunnel preached from the very difficult and little understood text. "There is a sin not unto death." Mr. Gunnell showed; that the difference between mortal, c'eath-bringing sin,. and sins which are forgiven, lay not in the heiniousness of the sin itself, but in the attitude of those who com- mitted the sin. The very murderers of Christ, because- they sinned through ignorance, were prayed for, that they might be forgiven; but for Judas, who had sinned' "against the Light," the condemnation was that " were better that, he had never been born." In the, evening in connection with the annual exchange of. pulpits among the Free Church Ministers,the Rov.J. L. Milne, B.O.; preached from the text "And behold, two of them went that same day to a village calledi Emmaus."

United Communion Service. The annual exchange of pulpits in connection with, the Evangelical Free Churches of Warrington and the. District took place on Sunday. In the evening a ,united. communion service was held in Bold-street Wesleyan Church. It was very well attended and was of an. interesting and impressive character. The Rev. J. Manning presided, and the address was given by the Rev. J. F. Matthews, who spoke on the controversies. associated with baptism and tke Lord's Supper,pointing out, however, with regard to the latter that there was one-common element believed in by all the churches-- the injunction of Christ " Do this in memory of Me," which focused the mind upon the central feature of their faith. That was the direct relation of Christ's death to human sin and guilt and its embodiment of the infinite love of our ever-present Godft set forth that love in its highest aspect. It was sacrificial in the beet sense.

Baptist Preachers' Association. The first of the monthly meetings of the Warrington and District Baptist Preachers' Association was held at Golborne-street on Monday evening when the President (the Rev. John Francis Matthews) lectured on the "Preacher's Equipment." The lecturer at • the. outset pointed out, that though nearly all the members. of that association were preachers and not pastors, the subject had as much interest for those of them who united both offices as for the others. The difficulties which the modern preacher had to face could only be estimated by observing (a) the amazing growth of the power of the Press for good and evil • (b) the indefinite extension of the reading public, and the general cheapening of litera- ture • (c) the rapid spread of compulsory education, and the gradual raising of the age-limit at which a scholar might leave school ; and (d) the specific training in scientific method, as compared with the absence of it five and twenty and thirty years ago. These facts made even the average demands upon the preacher greater than they had ever been. If, then, he was to command attention, if his message we% to go with power, to any audienoe whose intellectural attainments were higher than their father's were, their equipment for offensive. , and defensive work must be the best procurable. 2irst. they must study. Their work, was two-fold in char- acter. They had an evangel to proclaim, the written records of which they had to expound. Specializing in some one or two departments of Bible knowledge as Well as a general up-to-date, knowledg,,e of all that was said about the Book itself, in addition to an intimate acquaintance with its contents, was an absolute and permanent necessity. If to these a knowledge of the Hebrew and Greek versions, of the Old and New, Testaments were added, so. much the better. But the non-clerical preacher very often had little leisure to, pursue the study of a Biblical language. There were translations, commentaries, and encyclopmdies ex- pressly written for such. In so far as knowledge could be gained with a resort to the original text they could be far better equipped than the best persons in their congregations if they so desired. He would not have them tread daintily among words, Or specially pick and choose the simplest words they could. They might do that and still not be clear. Let them take care of their own personality. These were weighed up, labelled and docketed probably by every family which heard them preach. Let them not mistake that. However able, learned, eloquent they might be; however big a congregation they might command, the man outside the pulpit "told " far more than the man in it. "Be different outside, and your influence when preaching will count for nothing."

div.head: KIDNEY TROUBLE KNO IT,
div.p: KIDNEY TROUBLE KNO IT,

MY DEAR NIRCIII AND NiPHEWI,- . I must commence this week's letter by thanking you all for your kind wishes for the New Year. I trust that all of us will get a share of 1907's happiness, prosperity, and health; but, of course, a lot 'of it rests upon our, own exertions: We know that Fortune, etc., knocks at our doors but once, So we must make sure that we are at home when the time comes.

Well. I expect by the time my little rela- tions' eyes are scanning this letter, the holidays will all be over; and most of you looking for- ward to those to come. At the same time, I don't suppose many of you failed to take ad- vantage of those just past. I have received several letters with a description of how Christ- mas was spent, and from what I can see of it, some of you had a fine old time, and in the course of a week or two, if I get a few more contributions, I must devote one issue to pub- lishing the accounts and see who deserves the prize for the best description. I don't think that I have any fresh news this week, so I must close, with best remembrances, from
UNCLE NED.

. Dear 'Uncle Ned,—We are writing to thank you very much for the beautiful prizes you sent us. They came as a delightful treat on Thurs- day morning. Our " Gazette " this week came on Monday, not on Wednesday, as usual. We children were all in bed when it arrived, but we all called out, "Read what 'Uncle Ned' says," to mother. But mother said, "I cannot find it; perhaps he has been too busy, and has not been able to write one this week." Later on in the evening, after supper, when dada was reading the "Gazette," he all at once exclaimed, "Why, here's 'Uncle Ned's ' letter on the front Pan, and all our children have got a prize." He kept the secret all Christmas-day, until tea- time, when he pulled the " Gazette " out of his pocket, and read "Uncle Ned's " letter to us. 'I should almost think you could hear the " hurrahs " that went up when our names were read, where you live (we should love to know where).
We have had a joyous Christmas. Hope you have had the same, and we hope your little ones were pleased with the things the members of our Corner sent them.
Hoping you will have very many Happy New Years, with love,
We remain, your loving nephew and nieces, JAMES ASHTON KNIGHT. ALICE MABEL GLADYS KNIGHT. MARGARET CONSTANCE KNIGHT. HELENA DORIS KNIGHT.
REPLIES TO CONTRIBUTORS.

AMUR H.—l am glad you have rernind€(l me of my omission. I.hope you have received it by now. 'ANLEY H.—Thanks for poetry, Stanley; but it has already appeared in the " Corner." Still, never mind—" If at first you," ele. ALICE R.—lt is a very nice story, Alide; •but it is every so much too long. It would take up nearly a whole column. I am always pleased to receive anything short; in fact, the shorter the better. WILLIAM J. A.—l don't know how the printer came to leave out those two lines; but, then, printers are 'very, very naughty men, you know. -We- will forgive them this tin:l3. EVA S.—Many thanks for the small present just received. There are many who will be glad of them.

div.head: RIDDLES.
div.p: RIDDLES.

My first's a short sleep, my second's not more, My whole's an old iat, both behind and before. Now cut off my tail, and you'll find in my name An ancient and beautiful city of fame. My first's an exclamation, My second's a habitation, My third's a termination, My whole merits commendation,. WILLIAM JOSEPH ADAM.

Dear TJnele Ned,—l should like to become a member of your Children's Corner, but I do not know the rules. I enjoy reading the poetry very much. I recited a piece, called. "Papa's Letter," at our Band of Hope meeting, and they were very pleased with it. It was in the Corner a few weeks ago, and mother cut it out for me to learn, but I am sorry to say that I have lost it on my way to school. I have written a piece of poetry, which I should like you to accept for the Cdrner. I am just nine years old. Your loving Niece, , CLAIMER HEAP.
P.S.—My poetry is called "The Two Crossing Sweepers."
THE TWO CROSSING-SWEEPERS.

They could not claim a. single friend Beneath the widespread sky; But to each other they were bound • By poverty's strong tie. Though poor, they were too proud to beg; Too upright far to steal; And gladly would they sweep an clean, To gain an honest meal.

But, sad to say, the only food They often had to eat Was scraps of bread and broken fruit, They picked up from the street. It was a bleak and bitter morn, Just at the close of March, And they had slept the night before Within a market arch.

As very hungry, very cold, They wandered down the street, Joe picked an apple from the ground, And thought, "Why, here's a treat!" "It has been rather kicked about, But it's a good one still "; Arid, turning to his mate, he said, "What have you picked up, Will?"

div.head: WELCOME TO
div.p: WELCOME TO
Mildred E. Gosling, Nellie Effield, Clarrie Heap, Stanley Horxitt.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am now going to write you a short Christmas letter. Wishing you a merry Christmas and a happy New Year, hoping you will get a lot of Christmas cards from your nephews and nieces. I hope you are quite well, and all your nieces and nephews also. We have given up for •our Christmas holidays at Romanby School. We gave up on Thursday night for a fortnight, and we begin school on the day of my birthdayr-the Bth of January. There is going to be an extra market at North- allerton for Christmas. It is going to be to- morrow (Saturday). I am sending you a pair of cuffs for the poor, and. I will send you some other clothing for the poor later on. I am also sending a story called "The Old, Old Story," and I hope you .will like it, and I hope to see it in print. Dear Uncle Ned, a. year this Christ. mas I got a lovely book from you for a Christ- mas story, and I hope to do so this year. I think my brother is going to write to you also. I think I have no more to say. With many. Christmas wishes, I remain, your niece,
LILY COATES.
TEE OLD, OLD STORY.

Grandmother lives wilk-.1 the young Roonz.ins, and she is suah a dear old lady they all love her, for while their father and mother are away up .at the Abbey—Miehael RoonanG is Lady Darton's coachman, and Mrs. Roona.ns does the cooking there—she tells them Bible stories, asi wonderful as they are true. Shelah, Bridget, and Mike listen attentively, while Granny tells the old, old story of the baby Saviour's birth. in the lowly manger; how the star guided the wise men of the East, who cafne with rich value, to lay at the feet of the tiny Jesus, born to be King of Men, and ever since it has been called Christmas-day, in memory of the biith of Christ. LILIAN COATES.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l am now going to write you a short letter, and then I am going to t write you a story; Wiahing you a merry Christmaa and a jolly New Year, I will wri:te you a bigger letter next week. The story I am send- ing you is called—
AN APPLE PIE. A was an apple. pie. M mourned for it. B bit it. N nodded at it. Cent it, 0 opened it. D dealt it P reeped. in it.
D eat it. Q quartered it. F fought for it. R ran for it. G got it. S Mole it. H had it. T took it. 3" joined, as V viewed it. K kept it. W wanted it. L longed for it.
X Y Z and all wished for a piece in hand
GEORGE ERNEST COATES.

Dear Uncle Ned,—l received my box of choco- lates, with many, many thanks for sending me such a beautiful box, with which I am wiry pleased. I wish you a happy and prosperous New Year, lam sending you a small present, which r hope will be very useful to some little child. I am sending you a piece of poetry, which I hope to see in print, called—

div.head: CASTLES IN THE AIR.
div.p: CASTLES IN THE AIR.

When you and I are 'bigger, Fred, Say, what shall we do then? What shall we do with ourselves all day, When you and I are men? We'll climb the biggest poplar tree That stands against the wall; You could touch the stars from the top, I think, It is so straight and tall. We'll spread our bread and butter thick (And nurse shan't cut it then!) And have raspberry jam whenever we like, When you and I are men. We'll lo to bed quite late at night, And we won't get up till ten; And we'll never let Jane put the soap in our eyes, When you and I are men. And we'll have two white horses, Fred; One each for me and you; And we'll give up learning our A B C, And twice times one are two.

"Tim will take my bags to my room; let m• have some hot water."
"Yes, sir."
"What time is dinner ? " "The usual time, sir." • "Any company ? " "Captain Tennant, and is. and Miss Tennant." "What—Susie?"
"Yes, sir, Miss Susan. They are in the drawing- room."

"Very well," said Sir Humphrey. "I'll surprise the young dog, and dear old Tennant will be glad to see me," thought the ,naster of the house, as he climbed a thickly- carpeted staircase and made his way along broad, dimly-lighted corridors towards Harry's suite of rooms. When the petted youngster had returned from college his uncle had placed a corner of the right wing of the Hall at his disposal, to furnish and adapt for himself as he chose. Sir Humphrey rarely visited Harry in the young fellow's sanctum, not caring to criticise his nephew's mitre taste in the matter of engravings, and being unable to contem- plate it without remark. He hated to disagree with he lad. With increasing age he had come to regard harry as a son. He had, indeed, often said that aut for this feeling he might have macried and had son of his own.

Entering upon the landing that, led to Harry's private room, the door of which was open, Uncle Dakin received a shock that sent him staggering to the wall. A bullet could hardly have more com- pletely paralysed him for the moment; though he recovered presently, his teeth set, his hands zlenched.
"--- my uncle, I say!" There was no mistaking the voice. It was 11,7Y'L_

• "My dear Harry! " protested another, and this was Captain Tennant's voice. "I repeat it- him I'm sick of being nrollrht to book for a few trifling debts. Why the ieuce doesn't he die, ana let me have an innings before I'm too old to enjoy myself?" "Harry, my dear fellow," said Captain Tennant 'if you had not drunk more champagne than i goad for you, I should feel inclined never to forgive you for such a savage and ungrateful exclamation. " "Oh, bosh! What's the good of being heir to an estate, if you have to wait all your life to inherit?

"Your uncle has been awfully good to you." "He'd be awfully good to me if he'd peg out! I'll warrant you he should have as fine a funeral as the proudest corpse could desire." "Harry, you are mad!" "No, not mad, only frank. Some fellows think things they dare not voice. I say what I mean." "Then I'm develish sorry to hear it," said the other.

"There, don't be a fool, Tennant! Sit down, old chap. I dare say I'm an ungrateful beggar, but when one is heir to a millionaire, and every time one outruns the constable there is as much fuss as if he wasn't worth five hundred a year, it sets one's temper on edge. Hang it, I shouldn't wonder if the old brute lived to be a hundred!"
"Pray God he may! " said the other, evidently rising to his feet with anger. "I'll be hanged if I'll stay and listen to your ravings, drunk or sober."

"Oh, come; don't turn against a fellow. Your governor was poor as a church-mouse, so you can't appreciate the feelings of an expectant heir." "That's true; and I tell you plainly, Harry, that I should have despised myself if I had been tempted to desire my succession in the way you profess to desire yours." "Oh, well, forget what I've said. You led me into it by talking of the Jeffersons and Janet." "Then I'm sorry. If your uncle had ,the faintest idea that you did not love him as a father, by Jove, I think it would break his heart."

"No fools like old fools," said Harry. By this time Humphrey Dakin, who had been held as one spell-bound, felt himself sufficiently recovered to seek his own room. It is always interesting to know how a man comports himself in face of some tremendous discovery. If Sir Humphrey had been a Frenchman, he would probably have wept and torn his hair. An Oriental would have flung himself upon the floor and yelled. There are Englishmen, no doubt,_ who would have burst in upon their nepllew under similar circum- stances, and cut him off with a shilling, and so on. Sir Humphrey Dalin, though burning with indignation, walked calmly to his room, where he found Godwin laying out his clothes and waiting to shave him. "The Tenuants been here long ? " lie asked. "Most of the afternoon, sir," Godwin replied. "Mrs. Tennant has been with the gardener." "And Miss Susan ? " "With her mother, sir." "And Master Harry? In good form, as he calls it ? "
"Oh, yes, sir. Tie and the Captain have been in the cellar."
"To superintend Nixon's arrangement of the new bins, eh ? "

"I suppose so." "In vino veritas," said Sir Humphrey. "I can't say, sir, but I think it was the clarets that Nixon's new binning, sir." "Very well, that will do," Sir Humphrey replied. "Let them know I have arrived and am dressing." "Yes, sir," said Godwin, gliding from. the room.
Sir Humphrey went on dressing. His mind made up, he gave way to no vain regrets. It came to him like a flash what the nature of his. revenge should be.

The bell rang for dinner as he put on his rusty dress-coat and fastened his dingy black tie. "Wants me dead, does he?" he said, his face pale, his teeth clenched. "By Heaven, I'll shew him! I'll shew him!"

div.head: (Copyrght.) THE LOST HERITAGE.
div.p: (Copyrght.) THE LOST HERITAGE.
By JOSEPH HATTOIC,
Author of "Clyde," "Under the Great Seal," "By Order of the Czar," "When Greek Meeta Greek," "Cruel London," &c.

"What's come over Sir Humphrey ? " everybody was saying. And well they might wonder. Hitherto one of the most carelessly-dressed men in the eounty, Sir Humphrey Dakin had suddenly become quite a buck. Always distinguished-looking, despite his homespun and his weather-beaten hat, mar- riageable women had nevertheless ceased to angle for him, and girls had long since treated him as they might their grandfathers. • Ironmaster and territorial lord, Sir Humphrey was a man of great wealth. It was his nephew Harry whom match-making mothers encouraged in attentions to their daughters. Harry, a bold, extravagant, handsome young fellow, was publicly avowed as his uncle's heir. He was the son of Sir Humphrey's only tvother, who, preferring the Army to commerce, had succumbed in early life to the climate of the Gold Coast, and, his widow following him soon afterwards, left an only child, a boy of seven years. Hnmphrey adopted the lad, and had brought him up with every indulgence. Indeed, it may be said that ir Humphrey's ambition had gradually centred in his nephew Harry, who was in many things already master of Holmby Hall, except that Sir Humphrey now and then felt it necessary to assert his authority and to protest againat Harry's extravagance. All the time, however, it seemed as if lie were amassing wealth for his heir. It was shortly after a visit to London, on an important matter of business connected with the purchase of an estate adjacent to Holmby, that the change in Sir Humphrey's dress and manners became so marked as to elicit general remark. His man, Godwin, was bewildered-with the visits of tailors from town, and the city of Lincoln was taxed for haberdashery, boots, whips, sticks, and various articles that seemed more suitable for Harry than for Sir Humphrey._ But the uncle rut the nephew out, not only in dress but in the wearing thereof. Moreover, the old expression of serious- ness was gone from Sir Humphrey's face. His eyes were brighter than formerly, his step more elastic, and, among other feats, mental and physical, he had astonished his fellow county magnates by a speech at Quarter Sessions that argued a capacity for public life which had never been suspected. Indeed, Sir Humphrey was a new man. It was more particularly noted that he and his nephew were now seldom seen together. Formerly, when Harry was at home, the two were inseparable. They shot together, hunted together, and whenever they went to the county town they rode together and dined together at the County Club. Latterly, and suddenly, as we have said, all this was changed. The uncle, who had hitherto been tenderly regardful of his nephew's feelings, now took to bantering him on his faults; but what was surprising to Harry was the way in which Sir Humphrey laid himself out to be courteous and attentive to the ladies. He became especially devoted to Mrs. and Miss Tennant, and drova them with a party from Newark to the Lincoln Handicap in the smartest drag seen that day on the course. Harry affected to think that "the old man was in his dotitge " ; but Sir Humphrey was no longer the old man. To men of his own age, who compli- mented him on the revival of his youth, he would smile and talk of the elixir of life that an Eastern sage was selling in London at ten thousand pounds a bottle.

But all the- same, apart from the chief motive, Sir Humphrey had really fallen in love. Her name was Susan Tennant. She was the daughter of one of his oldest friends and neighbours, Captain Tom Tennant, a retired Army man, who had a small estate five miles from Holmby, which he found it difficult to maintain at its best on his limited income. Nevertheless, Valley Firm was a charm- ing place, with gardens that matched Sir Humphrey's own for choice fruits and flowers, and Mrs. Tennant presided over a table that might have been worthy of the most fastidious of gourmets; for she was a model housekeeper, proud of her establishment, though not too proud to take an active part in its management. Her kitchen knew her as intimately as her parlours; and while she might have earned her living, if need had been, as a cook or housekeeper, she could hold her own among the most fashionable women at the most fashionable functions. Sir Humphrey had always admired her, and more thihn once had suggested to Harry. that her only daughter, Susan Tennant, would make any fellow, rich or poor, a wife in a million. 1

Susan had all the charms of her mother, accentu- ated by youth. She was only three-and-twenty, and Sir Humphrey was sixty. If, a few months before he fell in love with her, anyone had forecast such a thing, he would have regarded the prophet as crazy. He had always been fond of Susan, Just as he had been fond of her father and mother, as an admiring friend and neighbour, and as one who had an honest appreciation of honest folk. But soon after the change people had noted in his dress and manner he began to see Susan's beauty in a new light. He had always known that her hair was a rich brown, with shades of bronze in the sunshine, that her face was fair beyond most others, that she had seaming eyes, a rosy cheek, a natural manner, and a voice that was musical. She rode with grace and freedom, and yet had none of those masculine characteristics that are affected by many women who follow the hounds and take an interest in manly sports. She was high- spirited, bright, and companionable; and one day, soon after the change, as we have said, Sir Humphrey Dakin fell in love with the girl; and before the day was over "spoke to her father," with what result we shall presently see. Meanwhile, let us discover to the reader the reason. why Sir Humphrey laid aside his old clothes and donned new ones, put, away his previously serious, if not austere, manner, and became a buck, challenging compariaon with the physical strength and alertness of yoking fellows who had known him for years as "old \Humphrey Dakin, young Dakin's rich and money-making uncle." The following chapter shall unravel the mystery; but it is our secret, Mind you; not a soul in Holmby or in the whole county has ever guessed it.

This is how it came to pass. Sir Humphrey had returned unexpectedly from town. "Master Harry in his room?" "Yes, sir.; Captain Tennant's with him. Pardon, sir, but we didn't expect you for nigh upon a week." "That's all right, Godwin; didn't look to have returned. • Glad. to get back, though. Don't say I've c.me;..l'd like to surprise Harry."

div.head: AN EX-POLICE COURT MISSIONARY.
div.p: AN EX-POLICE COURT MISSIONARY.
Some of His Trials and Hardships.

Mr. Cuthbert Shepherd, of Kenmure, Lancaster Gardens, Southend-on-Sea, is an earnest evangelist,who until lately was engaged in the trying work of a police- court missionary for the Rochford Hundred of Essex. His arduous and exacting duties some time ago told upon his health, and he became a victim tt) constipation. That he is now strong and well again is due entirely to bile beans. "At times I hardly knew what to do with myself," Mr. Shepherd told a Southend journalist "If I was not in acute pain I was very drowsy, and my work was extremely irksome. I had acute pains in the head, which prevented me from sleeping, and when I did manage to lose, consciousness my slumber was so heavy that when I woke I felt weary and unrefreshed. "Cycling and walking had been two of my favourite pursuits, hut I was unable to take any interest in either. I had always been a hearty eater, but often I had a positive distaste for food, and after every meal there was a fresh attack of the pains in the head and the drowsy feeling that almost incapacitated ' me. I tried all sorts of remedies, but I could discover nothing to give me permanent relief until ,I was persuaded to try bile beans. "Within a short time after commencing with bile beans a feeling of renewed life came into me, such as I had not experienced for many years. The pains and drowsiness vanished, refreshing sleep took the place of restless nights, and I could eat and enjoy my food. I continued with bile beans until I was quite free from those conditions that had before so severely hapdicapped me. lam now in perfect health. Being so wMI known through my public work as a police-court missionary and a lay evangelist, I feel that the great benefit I have derived from bile beans might lead to the same good being derived by others who are suffering so I give the Bile Bean Co., full permission to use my testimonial for this end." Be guided by Mr. Shepherd's experience ; see that you get the genuine remedy. All chemists stock Bile Beans, at one-and-three-halfpence per box, or two-and- threepence for family size, containing three times the quantity.

Sir Humphrey was quite gay over dinner. At least,. he thought he was. He was very attentive to Mrs. and Miss Tennant, and confidential with the entire table. He joked Harry about Mild Jefferson. Never, before had he mentioned her name. He didn't like the Jeffersons. Mrs. Jefferson was a notorious match-making mamma, and small blame to her, seeing that she had six marriageable girls, with fashionable tastes and the smallest •of dowries. Harry hated his uncle to think he cared for Janet., one of the showiest, not to say fastest, of young women, who brought into the county all the lively and unrestrained manners of town; rode a bicycle in bloomers, and at the last County Ball had been shamefully conspicuous in a dress that might have rivalled a Trouville bathing costume. It was very unusual for ir Humphrey to speak of his business Or his mone . Over this memorable dinner he put aside all his customary reticence. He informed Harry that he had concluded the Purchase of the adjacent estate which it had been his life-long ambition to add, to the Holltiby acre., In a loud aide he acquainted Tennant With the fact that his Cleveland iroh property had gone up enormously in talne. To Mrs. Tennant he said : "My dear friend, there is a deal of talk about Millionaires in these days, and yet they are common enough—you have 'one for your neigh- bour. If I was wound up to=day my estate would realise over two millions—that's what those ghouls, the lawyers, will call cutting up well, when they come to read my last testament to the assembled heirs And assigns, or whatever the legal jargon may be for my succ4sors." "My dear Sir Humphrey, we should value you none the leas if your estate was as modest as our own ; and as'for• • cutting ;up,' as the legal men have it., you have many and iminy along year before you—enough to become a triple millionaire." "What do you say, Susie? " the old man asked. "I'm sure I hope so,, Sir Humphrey.' "That I'm sure you do, my child ; and permit an old fallow to say that he never saw you look more charming." -- "Thank you, Sir Humphrey. But you always are so kind," the girl replied ; and shortly afterwards the ladies retired. The men had a general chat over their coffee, abot),t the crops that had been gathered and the prospects of pheasant shooting. Harry said the keeper assured him they had ten thousand birds in the covers, and promised him fine sport. "I have invited half-a-dozen fellows for the First," said Harry; lighting a fresh cigar—he never smoked a weed more than half through, following the example of a discreet and generous Prince. "That's right, Trarry .; the more the merrier," said Sir HuMphrey..... " Make hay while the sun shines,' is a good motto, and ' Gather ye rosebuds while ye may, Old Time will still be flying,' or words to that effect, is goo4l poetry; and there may be some truth in the proyerb. No fools like old fools.' One never knows what a day may bring forth."
Harry went to bed wondering what the deuce was the matter with the old man.

And so it came to pass that Sir Humphrey entertained a score of tailors, and brushed back his hair from his broad forehead, and rode to hounds in the trimmest costume and on the rarest of mares; made calls, went to dinners, and, people said, grew younger every day. Harry Dakin came and went at his own sweet will. His uncle paid his debts and made no complaints; but the young fellow gradually felt that he had somehow lost his confidence. The old man, by careful observation, discovered ample confirmation of the reality of Harry's ingratitude. A well-known Jew money-lender, who knew the ways of the world, had thought it advisable to consult Sir Humphrey in regard to certain loans he had miUle to his heir, secured by deeds that chewed too plainly how largely Harry had already discounted, his death; an,fl it was not by his own seeking that he had learnt when.: most of the money went, despite the young fellow's professed love for Janet Jefferson. The establishment was not in that favourite region of the cheap novelist, St. John's Wood, but in the very heart of the most aristocratic localities of the West End of town.

As Sir Humphrey grew in knowledge of his nephew's unworthiness, he seemed to rejoice, as one who had been spared a bitter sorrow; for with his disappointment had crept into his lonely heart the warming light of love. "I know you are young enough to be my daughter, my child," he said, "and I would not have ventured to speak to you without I the per- mission of your mother, one of iny very dearest friends, and possibly the best woman that ever lived; nor if I did not love you as fervently as if we were both of an age." They were sitting together in the morning-room of Valley Farm, and it was spring. The haw- thorn was white in the hedges, and the -perfume of gillyflowers came in at the open window. Her hand lay in his, her face was flushed, her words trembled on her hos. "You are very good to me," she said. "Yes, my dear, but that is not the question. We have always been great friends, have we not ? " "Always," and her soft fingers tightened a little on his strong hand. "What 1 want to ask you is this. Do you think you could leave your mother and father and come and live with me at Holmby, and be the mistress of it, and—be my wife—and love me?" .Sir Humphrey trembled with anxiety; and it was strange, but when she looked up at him to make reply she saw that there were tears in his eyes. He bent his head, that she might not note them.

"I have always loved you, Sir Humphrey Dakin," the girl replied, in the clear tones of truth, "ever since I-was a child, and now that I am a woman I will be your wife." "My' darling! " he said, taking her into his arms. "And I will be your slave!"

And so he was, but she led him in a silken chain. When the day of the wedding was appointed, Sir Humphrey called Harry to his room and said "Listen, Harry. I will not upbraid you, I leave you to your own' conscience. I have settled a thousand a year upon you. My lawyers, receiving from y 0,.. a complete schedule of your debts, will pay them, so that you start with an unencumbered twenty pounds a week as long as you live. And now I want you to clear out. You are no longer heir to Holmby, so you will not be troubled with a harassing expectancy of my death. I don't mean to die until lam a hundred. Anyhow, I hope to have a son of my own, who shall be brought up :o work and earn his own living like a gentleman, so that he need not worry himself about dead men's shoes.' Good-bye! It is very hard, no doubt," said Mrs. Jefferson, to whom Harry went for consolation and advice, "but you have played your cards very badly." "That cur, Tennant, must have repeated what I said."

"No doubt," Mrs. Jefferson replied. "You should not have barked until you could bite. Of zourse, as regards Janet, that is all off; a thousand s year between, you and Janet is no good. If I were you, I should go to America or somewhere— they say New Guinea is a, very possible country— iig for gold, or keep a '-ranch, or something in which young men make what the Americans call • their pile' or hide their failure. I am a woman Df the world, and now you must be a man of the world. You have said good-bye to your uncle, you must now say good-bye to us. Janet, by the way, has gone on a visit to some friends in the Engadine." Talk of May and December, you should see how they flourish together at Holmby Hall—December rich and sturdy as October, May full-blown, with the warmth of summer in her hair 1 If ever the Divinity designed that there should be a paradise on earth, you have exemplification of it at Holmby Hall ; a hale, hearty man of merely middle age, as it might seem, though getting on for seventy, with a wife beautiful in her womanhood, and who honours and loves him with all her heart—the twain rich in heirs and heiresses, to succeed to millions and the responsibilities of wealth, a happy, healthful family, each of whom is a fairy godmother or a Santa Claus to half the county at Christmas, and at all times a blessing to the poor. [Tull END. I

div.head: RELIEF TO ASTHMATICS.
div.p: RELIEF TO ASTHMATICS.

While it is probably true that there is no certain care for Asthma, Angier's Emulsion always gives relief, more especially when there are bronchial or catarrhal complications. In both chronic and acute cases it affords great comfort by soothing the lungs and air passages, and by restoring strength to the exhausted system after the paroxysms.
