Mr. J. H. Westbrook complained of the condition of Mitchell-street and Farrell-road, and said there was enough water in them at times to drown a:child. It was decided that all streets and passages which needed cindering be cindered, the work to be done to the satisfaction of the Surueyor.

Garden • Society Annual Meeting. The annual meeting of the Stockton Heath Garden Society was held in the Hall Cafe, Victoria-square, on Tuesday evening, Mr. Charles Plinston presiding over a good attendance. Mr. Vere B. Davies was re-appointed president; the Revs. H. V. Pigot and J. Collins, Dr. Parker and Messrs. L. G. Davies, A. J. Willett, W. H. J; Jenkins, Roger C. Parr, and J. H. Clarke vice-presidents; Mr. C. Plinston. hon. treasurer; and Mr. A. Fewcett, hon. secretary ; the usual votes of thanks being accorded to the officials for the valuable services rendered by them during the past 12 months. The committee were constituted as follows :—Messrs. A. Broady, F. Broady, W. Downes, T. Edden, John Hallows, J. Moore, J. Mynekyme, W. H. E. Noden, John Peters, J. Ryan, F. Timperley, W. A. Timperley, E. Vernon, W. H. Woodcock, W. Skelton, F. Pearson, McDermott, W. Leach, J. H. Fletcher, George White, W. Hickman and E. Bindloss. _ _ _

The report of the committee, read by the S6cretary, was adopted. It stated that the year had been a succesful one, The membership had increased from 312 to 490, which was fairly satisfactory. Three shows had been held. In March the first bulb show of the society was held, and for a first effort was a success, the quality of the exhibits being quite up to the average. The general show in August was undoubtedly the best ever held. The entries, 580, were over double those of the previous year, and were of a much -higher standard of merit, and the attendance formed a record. The autumn show of outdoor chrysanthemums surpassed previous efforts. Numerous visits had been paid to the gardens of gentry in the neighbourhood, and were largely, attended. The winter monthly meetings had been any- thing but well-attended, and the committee had to con- sider the advisability of discontinuing them as the labour and the expense were considerable, and not justified by the appreciation shown:, The committee had decided to form a juvenile branch to encourage the children of the district to cultivate small garden plots. They hoped that would add considerably to the interest taken in the society. It was the ambition of the com- mittee to make the society the best in the district. They thanked all Who had in any way assisted the society at the shows and in other directions. Lady Greenall wrote to say that she would be very pleased to give any special prizes as last year, and should also like to give some prizes in the children's section. She would give first prizes all through that section if the society wished. (Applause.)

div.p: 'LETTERS TO THE EDITOR.

NOTICE TO CORRESPONDENTS. Authors of letters intended for publication must in all cases send their names and addresses to the Editor as a guarantee of good faith. ALFRED STA:max.—The affairs cif Alfred Stanway Ltd. hardly seem to us proper matter for discussion in the P ress.—E D. "Ex."

*How to Fight Socialistic Legislation. Sir,—The short interval between the late Autumn Session cud the coming Session of 1967 barely gives us breathing time before we are again flooded with vote- hunting measures contemplated no doubt by the Govern- ment, plus the private members' Bills that will be sup- ported, or taken up by the Government. Knowing then ss we do from past experience the trend of the policy of this, and indeed of all Governaients since 1870, it would be well to inquire how far the Administration of the day fulfills the object and duties of Government. To what end do we pay our Secretaries of State £5,000 a year? Is it to enslave us with bripectors and inspectresses and hamper industry by restrictions on trade and labour, plus interference with contract, and the transfer of property, and property rights, from the less numerous to the more numerous voting classes of the Nation? Or is it, as I have heard in bygone years a Liberal Attorney-General declare it to be, the primary duty of Government to maintain and secuce our liberty and property of all kinds, including a Briton's free right—using Lord Bramwell's famous words—" to bestow his labour and his talents as seem to him best," a right practically taken away by the Trade Disputes Act of last Session ? That Act now allows picketing that need not be peaceful, and which cap only be met, in the interests of the liberty of labour and trade, by the counter picketing of pickets—a course for which an efficient organisation already exists. Well, such being the primary duty of Government, it is needless, looking to the Socialistic vote-hunting measures that have been passed, and not resisted by the so-called Opposition, both parties striving to retain or gain the support of the Socialist Labour Party, whose avowed object is the doing away with individual liberty and the absorption of property of all kinds into the hands of a Labour Governed State,it is,as said, needless to inquire how far the two main parties in the State when holding the reins of power have fulfilled that • duty. Their measures and actions give a clear and • definite answer. Where then is there a remedy for this state of things to be found? To whom can we look? The Duke of Devonshire will not, I fear, move. Lord Rosebery - seems inclined to •remain in his lonely furrow, from which the Scots Greys alone have been able momentarily to move him. Whither shall we turn? To whom shall we appeal? Why to all true Britons who love liberty, who are in favyur of private as against State-owned property, and who are prepared to stand by indi- vidualism with its endless chances of success in life, - and resist the coming of the dead level of Socialism so repugnant to the feelings of free men. •Yes ! let all such band themselves together irrespective of party and strive by their votes to give effect to principles which all Governments know to be sound, but have not the courage to support. Meetings should be held alike in • country and in town, and Anti-Socialist defence associa- tions formed that will steadily resist all Socialistic measures no matter whence they come.—Yours faith- fully,
WEIVYSS,
Gosfo-rd, Longniddry, N.B. January 15th, 1907.

div.head: NEW THEATRE.
div.p: THE NEW THEATRE.

Public interest in the new theatre project has been . stimulated during the week by the erection on the site off Barbauld-street of a notice board bearing an • intimation that a Palace Theatre and Hippodrome is to be built there immediately and opened as early as possible in 1907. While still awaiting an official announcement on the subject, we understand that the undertaking is being launched by a prominent • Yorkshire 'firm who are the proprietors of many similar theatres in that county. Plans are already being prepared and the building will be on the most up-to-date lines. We understand that the firm have booked Parr Hall for five weeks, and will present variety entertainments at an early date.

div.head: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS.
div.p: LIBERAL WARD MEETINGS.
FAIRFIELD WARD.

The annual meeting of the Fairfield Ward Committee was held in Fairtiold schools on Tuesday evening and was lar,gely attended. In the absence of Mr. George 'Walker (chairman of the committee) the proceedings were presided over by Mr. J. T. Locker. The following . officers were elected :—Chairman, Mr. George Walker; vice-chairmen, Councillor Duncan, Rev. H. Wall, Messrs. W. Haigh, B. Farrar, J. T. Locker, and J. Griffiths; lion. secretaries, Mr. William Habberley, and Mr. G. T. Rushton. A hearty vote of thanks was accorded to e officers for their past services. WHITECROSS WARD.

There was an exceptienally good attendance at the -meeting of the Liberal Committee of this Ward, which was held in Thewlis-street schools on Wednesday even- ing. Councillor James Evans, J.P., presided. Letters of apology for non-attendance were ,received from -zeveral members of the committee.—Resolutions of sympathy with the relatives of the late Mr. Bernard Percival and Mr. J. Mercer were passed, the members standing as a mark of respect. The following officers were elected :—Chairman, Councillor James Evans, .J.P.; vize-chairmen, Councillor Thomas Barton, Messrs. Henry Roberts, J.P., Nathan Cook, William Wright and William Clatworthy ; hon. secretaries, Mr. James T. Barton and Mr. R. W. Cook. The casual vacancy in the representation of the ward caused by the death of Coun- oillor Brough, was discussed, and a deputation was appointed to wait upon several gentlemen. We understand that Mr. Henry Roberts, J.P., is one of the gentlemen who have been waited upon by the -deputation. A further meeting of the Ward Committee Nvill be held on Monday.

div.head: TEMP ERANCE MISSION. MRS. JENNIE WALKER'S VISIT TO WARRINGTON.
div.p: TEMP ERANCE MISSION. MRS. JENNIE WALKER'S VISIT TO WARRINGTON.

Mrs. Jennie Walker, of London, who has a world- wide reputation as a temperance orator, has this week conducted a successful mission in the Bold-street Wesleyan schoolroom. The Warrington lodges of the International Order of Good Templars—a flourishing organization which is doing a good work in the town —were responsible for the arrangement of the campaign and the members took a great interest in the effort. There was a large attendance at • ing meeting which was held on Tuesday evening. The proceedings began with a reception when many local temperance wcrkers.took the opportunity of welcoming Mrs. Walker. In the absence through indisposition of Mr. James Dodds, the meeting was presided over by Mrs. Dodds who said she was placed to welcome Mrs. Walker, and also to know that she (Mrs. Dodds) counted one in that great army of men and women who were marching on to try and destroy the dreadful curse of drink. They read in the Prophets how they loved to talk about old men dreaming dreams and young men seeing visions. "We still dream dreams and still see visions," continued Mrs. Dodds, "but we are not obedient to them." Mrs. Dodds related the story of Dr. Bernardo, and his obed- ience to his vision. Throught his instrn- mentality more than 50,000 waifs and strays were rescued from the the gutter of sin, drink and misery and won to honest, faithful lives. It might be,shesaid,that during the present mission some young men and women might see a -vision of what God needed them to do. Would they be true, and come and help those who were toiling in the temperance cause in Warrington? Mrs. WALKER is an eloquent and forcible speaker and she dealt in a most entertaining manner with the subject " Past and present." They were met, she said, to declare war against the enemy, strong drink. They were going to do their best in three nights to make it known and felt that there was an organization in exist- ence, and that there was enough temperance sentiment in the town, and enough deep interest in the cause to band themselves together to make a strong force, not only during the three days, but throughout the remain- ing time liquor was with them. They would make the liquor traffic tremble. "I am not a waxwork doll for you to come and look at," continued Mrs. Walker, amid laughter, "and I have not come here to talk plati- tudes. We are here to work." Mrs. Walker said that for twenty-six years she had travelled in this and other countries doing her best to smite the enemy strong drink, of which she had a keen hatred. She spoke of the progress which the temperance movement had made since the seven men of Preston declared war on drink, and added, "It will go on until the people have the power to veto the traffic." Great and wonderful changes had been made, but she thought they had not worked as assiduously as they might have done. It was significant that at licensing banquets the speakers told them that people were becoming more sober, and that drinking got less. They would all like to see those engaged in the trade occupying the places of the unemployed. There was as much need for temperance meetings to-day as ever. Educational work should be done until the electorate was sufficiently enlightened to demand the suppression of the traffic. In the early days of the temperance movement they were called "water drinkers," were told they had water on the brain." Now times had changed, and temperance people were in the majority instead of the minority. They no longer had to make excuse for their principles, and they realized that they had a principle adopted on science, Bible, love and truth. (Applause). At one time it was thought that to drink cold water would be ruinous to the constitution. Now the valuable properties of cold water were recognized. "Plenty of water inside and out will make you wealthy, healthy and stout." (Laughter.) The taking of alcohol was formly regarded as beneficial,now it was considered foreign matter and poison to the brain and nerve. Sparkling water brought peace, happiness and gladness into the lives of the toilers.Mrs.Walker paid a tribute to the Salvation Army which was doing a magnificent work on total abstinence lines. The very best of the medical faculty were undivided in their opinion that liquor was un necessary in health or sickness. The brewers claimed to be the benefactors of the nation, and asked where would the revenue come if their industry ceased. If the 'liquor traffic ceased to-morrow the nation would be purer, healthier, and certainly wealthier. (Applause.) The drink habit was a selfish habit, and the cause of thousands of children starving. She claimed that people owed it as a duty to themselves and to the cause to be total abstainers. Even the persons who took liquor in small quantities were never at their best. They must also realize their responsibilies in regard to those who were being injured physically and spiritually through the drink interest. _ _ .
.-...... _____ During the meeting hymns were sung. Mr. Levi Richardson gave the solo, "Come unto Me," Mr. E. Wilkes accompanying. A WOMAN'S QUESTION.

On Wednesday afternoon Mrs. Walker dealt particu- larly with woman's part in the temperance work. There was a good attendance of ladies. Miss Bessie Dutton presiding. In the course of a brief introductory address Miss DUTTON urged the need for greater enthusiasm in the work. If they believed what they professed they must put their best into the work. They must not allow their minds to be filled with bright, sparkling and beautiful thoughts alone but they must carry those thoughts into practice in their lives and influence. (Applause.) Mrs. WALKER said that one of the many reasons why the United States and Canada were ahead of England in temperance work was because the women of those two nations had become keenly and definitely inter- ested in the question, and when the women of England regarded it as did the women across the water they would go up by leaps and bounds. The women of the great American continent realized that a sound mind and a sound body were the birthright of their children and an association, which was rapidly growing in strength, had been formed in which the young women pledged themselves not to marry men who took intoxicating liquors. Surely they in England ought to go as far as that, as if there was one question before them, and before every other nation, it was the question of the child life. The child was the one centre of influence—the pivot upon which everything turned. The child, morally, physically and mentally was in danger, not because they had not enough schools, but because there was something wrong—and that something legislators would not be able to set right without the co-operation of women. "She who rocked the cradle ruled the world." How deeply that should be stamped upon the hearts of the women. It was the women who had charge of the nursing of the children of the land to-day who trained the men who would stand in the senate house to-morrow, or would be found in a criminal's dock. What the women of to-day were so woaid the people of the country be to-morrow. What the women imprinted upon the lives of the chil- dren that would the children say to-morrow, and she would say to the women be sober. They might legis- late if they liked, but if the hearthstone were degraded with drink so surely would the life of the nation be ruined. Women never, in the history of the world, gave herself more to intemperance than to-day, and they must arouse themselves from their indifference and put on their armour to go and fight England's foe (Applause).

div.head: "ONLY A GLASS."
div.p: "ONLY A GLASS."

There was a larger attendance on Wednesday evening, when Mrs. Walker lectured, on "Only a glass." The chair was occupied by Mr. R. D. Petterson, D.0.T., of Liverpool, who was supported on the platform by the Rev. J. S. Hughes, Mrs. Simpson, Mr. C. E. Parker and others.

The CHAIRMAN said that the Good Templam believed in the fatherhood of God and the brotherhood of man. In the Good Templar lodges they followed up the work done by public missions and tried to get hold of those who had been victims of intemperance and make a home for them where they would always be amongst friends and be free from temptation. (Applause). Mrs. WALKER prefaced her lecture by commending the Good Templary movement and pointed out that its objects were total abstinence for the individual and prohibition for the State. She believed that God was able to bring about the day when the liquor traffic should be swept away. (Applause). They who understood the power of the liquor traffic said there was no place for strong drink but out of the way of the people. Good Templary first gave women equal rights with men, recognizing that they were quite able to take the same part in meetings. As a counter-attraction to the public house, the work of the lodges was invaluable. Passing on to the subject of the lecture, Mrs. Walker dealt with the question of moderation. A very large number of people thought they had a perfect right to take" a little drop "and that the temperance cause did not exist for them but only for the drunkard. She could assure them that if in Warrington they could get over to the side of total abstinence all the "one glassers " they would indeed have a rare big army of teetotallers. (Applause). The liquor men in this town would tremble and think the world was coming to an end. Temperance workers talked too much about the drunkard and top little about the " little droppers." The total abstainer was on the right side—and that was the great thing. (Applause). No- one intended to become a drunkard when he started as I a moderate drinker. Alcohol was a poison whether it I was taken in large or small quantities. People who took I small quantities were slowly but surely poisoning their system. Health was largely within our own power to obtain and keep, and the workingmen and women had their only capital in sound, good health. If the liquor shops were closed, the people would undergo a remark- able change in their physical condition. There was only one right side and that was the safe side—not to touch the first glass. Liquor was no respecter of per- sons—its only redeeming feature was that it served everybody alike. She had faith in legislation— especially if they would send a woman or two to Parliament. (Laughter and applause). She had faith in many of the men who were sitting in the House of Commons and she believed the educational work which was going on in the country in relation to legislation was all in the right direction. She had faith

div.head: PROGRESS OF EMMANUEL CHURCH.
div.p: THE PROGRESS OF EMMANUEL CHURCH.
Interesting Review at the Annual Tea Meeting.

One of the most pleasant functions of the year in connection with Emmanuel Church is the annual con- gregational tea party and entertainment. Exceptionally gratifying success attended this year's gathering which took place in the Institute, Knutsford-road, on Thursday evening and there were many indications of the increased prosperity of the church and the varied branches of its work. Nearly 200 members of the congregation and friends sat down to tea, the following ladies presiding at the tables :—Ars. Vaughan, Mrs. Norman, Mrs. E. Allen, Mrs. Armstrong, Miss Allen,Mrs. Atherton, Mrs. Brovvn,Mrs. William Dickens, Mrs. Landon, Miss Hodge and Miss Straw. B3fore the concert began, the incumbent (Rev. F. VAUGHAN) spoke at some length on the work of the church. He said that gathering was another evidence of the strong element of unity and sympathy in Christian interest which was continually manifest in Emmanuel Church. They were now twenty-six years old and he thought the present gathering, like many similar meetings in years gone by, justified their claim to their majority and seemed to give promise of a few years of life yet to •come. (Applause). He was glad to be able to announce that their communicants' list, which was the one sure test of membership, contained the names of 160 persons who had willingly entered into fellowship with the Church and gathered round the Lord's Table. The Sunday School numbered about 25) scholars and good work was being done amongst the men. All these things showed that the Church was increasing and that the year had been one of progress (Applause.) So far as the finances were concerned, the position was helpful and encouraging. With regard to the Institute, they had paid all the interest which was due up-to-date on borrowed money and had begun to pay off the capital. They meant to ply their debt and to increase their numbers and to bring as much sunshine and gladness as possible into the homes of the people. (Applause.) They must look forward to the day when, having paid off the debt on the Church and Institute, they might possibly open a Church somewhere else and hand down their heritage of Protestant tnuth, liberty and freedom. (Applause.) Let them adopt the watch- word of Bishop Cummins—"Go forward and do a noble work." They were not heresy hunters ; they were not like so many terrier dogs hunting out the rats in the old family dwelling. Their first great object was soul. saving. He hoped in the near future to do something for the lads. He believed that in the churches of the land there was a great leakage between the senior boys and the men and he had it on good authority that only ten out of every 100 children in the Sunday schools became bona fide members of the churches in which they were reared. It was saddening to see the number of lads congregated outside public houses and at street corners and indulging in conversation which was far from elevating. The great need was for a social element and environment which would uplift the lads. Mr. Vaughan impressed upon his hearers the necessity for stability and, replying to those who had criticised him for taking up the work in that neighbourhood, said they were there as Reformed Episcopal Churchmen for conscience sake. (Applause). An enjoyable programme was then submitted, includ- ing several excellent glees by the choir, songs by Miss Armstrong, Miss Cruikshank, Miss Torakinson, Mr. Tynan, Mr. Grounds, duets by Messrs. Atkinson and Grounds, picolo solos by Mr. Tomkinson, and cornet solos by Mr. Peterson. Miss Nelly Gandy accompanied. Mr. D. HODGE, who occupied a place beside the Chairman addressed the meeting during the interval. A large meeting such as that, he said, pointed to a strong family feeling inithe church, and augured well for their future prosperity. He could see no reason why in the near future Emmanuel Church should not find its true place in the forefront of the Christian work of the town. Referring to their minister, the speaker said that Scotchmen had the name of being severe critics of sermons and preachers, and as one of these, he should like to express his opinion that the pulpit of Emmanuel Church was as well supplied as any could possibly be. (Applause.) His advise was" Take good care of a good man now you've got him." There was no reason why thus led they might not increase and develop their excellent and needful work. (Applause.) Mr. W. Dicims, churchwarden, nioved a hearty vote of thanks to all who had contributed to the success and enjoyment of the evening. This was seconded by Mr. W. ATHERTON, minister's warden, and carried with acclamation. The meeting closed with the Doxology and Benediction.

Mrs. Bennett, aged 79, a widow, who resided with her son-in-law, Mr. Snowden, stationmaster at Cayton, near Scrrborough, was killed at Cayton on Wednesday. She was crossing the line at the station when she was knocked down ey the 2,30 train from Scarborough to Hull and was killed instantly.

div.head: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
div.p: RUGBY FOOTBALL.
[By " Ovalist."]

Well won Warrington ! That was a fine victory at Hull on Saturday and it showed the Warrington team at its best. They were hardly expected to succeed where Broughton Rangers failed the week before—especially with a comparatively week team— but determination and grit did the trick in the end. Warrington are rewarded by being third in the League table, and their chances of finally being found in the first four are immeasurably improved. On the form they are showing just now the League Champion- ship is by no means out of reach and the" Wire- pullers " must be considered serious competitors for the cup and medals. By and by some of the cripples will be fit again. The opposition may then look out for squalls, for I am convinced that the Warrington club possesses the finest team in Lancashire.

There is understood to have been a bonus offered the Warrington men to secure full points at Hull, and whether that did the trick or not is a problem. I remember a similar inducement being offered the men at Broughton earlier in the season, with the result that they got so excited at the prospect of ease and luxury held before their eyes that they quite failed to do themselves justice. On Saturday at Hull they kept their heads, and showed just that solidity at critical moments which was required to bring them through a severe struggle. Twice there was only a point between the teams, and that was the margin at the finish, so that it may be imagined the fight was somewhat sanguinary at times. Hull had counted upon a certain victory as a reward for their improved form, and the grim resolution of Warrington not to be beaten proved rather painful to the well-intentioned third-porters. It was something like the lamb being led to the sacrificial altar and then turning and pole- axing the executioner. Of course I know that the metaphor is a bit mixed, and that there is nothing lamb-like about the Warrington thirteen but it will serve to show that the good folk of Hull were mildly surprised.

There was really not much to choose between the teams. In fact, the losers played the prettier football on the whole,but while their passing was neat it was not so dangerous as that of the Warrington men. The latter attacked suddenly and frequently and ought to have had four tries instead of two,while the defensive work of Berry,Tilley,and Isherwood was first-class. Not a man failed, and the tackling was something to tremble at. The game was more like a cup-tie in fact, and aroused so much excitement that the rEferee got mobbed at the close by the disappointed Hull partizans. Much of the praise for the victory is due to Lees and Jenkins who performed brilliantly, the last-named coming out in a new light by the way he upset the home team's combination. Berry was also in magnifi- cent form, though he could not be said to give the lead to Taylor, who played a great game for Hull. The forwards were well-matched, with the Warring- ton six showing rather the more dash and " devil." Thomas and Heath were ever in the front, and the former showed clever judgment near the close when he ran into the thick of the Hull men rather than kick and risk giving the chance of the " mark," or drop-kick which the other side was waiting for.

Hull had three shots at goal in the last stages, but Fortune was on Warrington's side for once and the ball went astray. This was lucky, for Warrington could not get a goal and Preston was much missed in this department. Berry has been so long out of practice at place kicking that he missed two easy attempts. One does not like criticising a winning side, but the fact was apparent that Tilley is n)t fast enough for threequarter play, though he shone on the defence on Saturday, and Hockenhall was only a moderate success. When Fish, Dickenson and Taylor are all fit it will be a problem whom to leave out. The advantage ought to be found in giving a man an occasional rest, which some of them could do with now, I dare say. Brooks has had a lot of knocking about, but he keeps up his dash splendidly.
The League Table up-to-date is as follows : For Agst. Per- _ _

Warringtpn are now in the happy pnsition of being third —a pot of honour they have won by sheer merit, for )ao club has a heavier fixture list, while Runcorn has a much lighter one. They will have to keep hard at it, however, to maintain a place among the favoured four, for after to-day there are four matches away in succession, viz., Oldham, Widnes, Huddersaeld and Halifax. Fortunately there is reason to hope that both Taylor and Dickenson will be fit next week, so that there should be a fair prosnect of points wherever the team ,goes. Fish should not be long after, and by the time the Cup-ties commence Warrington ought to be in possession of a team fit to lick creation—or go down in round 1.

The return match with Bradford to-day should be an attractive fixture, for the Park Avenue men have been sharers in some heroic struggles on the Wilders- pool ground. Less than a month ago Warrington snatched a victory at Park Avenue and they should be equal to repeating the performance to-day, especi- ally as practically the same team will be doing duty. There is only one change from last week, Preston taking the place of Harmer. By the way, I still think Forster deserves a chance in superior company. He was the best forward on the field last Saturday at Warrington, and seeing that we have plenty of weight his speed and resource would be of use. No man has the knack of following the ball better and snapping up stray chances to score. For the past two year's now, much better use might have been made of the old threequarter's services.

The selected team to play Bradford i: Berry, full back ; Brooks, Tilley, Isherwood and Hockenhall, threequarters ; Lees and Jenkins, half backs; Boardman Preston, Thomas, Heath, Naylor and Shugars, Boardman,

I see that G. 11. Marsden has definitely retired from the game, and the announcement must be an addi- tional Mow to Bradford. An international half back is not easily replaced, and Marsden was one of the best in the IT.nion.
Many of the old Warrington supporters will regret to hear of the death this week of H. Higginbottom who used to play half-back for the first team in the days of "Smack" Hato and W. Houghton.

, Sam Johnson has gone to Wigan and not Warring- ton. This will be bad news to the Wilderspool crowd, but it must be understood that Wigan have the longer purse and were prepared to dip further into it. Another item is that Frank Harry is turning out again for Broughton. Association Football.

The Warrington Albions disappointed their supporters on Saturday, even if the result of the cup- tie with Oughtrington Park was no great surprise. It was hoped that for once in a way Albions would master the Parkites, but after opening well they fell away and were badly beaten 1-1. As this was on the •Albions' ground the local disappointment was keen, though a :e1.7 gate proved some compensation. It is cuicus that the Albions played best against the wind in the first half and were ineffective in the second. The Parkites played a very resolute cup-tie game. Mather and Thomason being especially danger- ous, and fully deserved their entry into the next round.

div.p: in the Church of the Living God if it would remove the trammels which held it bound hand and foot to the paralysing agency of strong drink. But she had much more faith in the firm uncompromising example of the father and mother in the home. (Applause.) Continuing Mrs. Walker said that thousands had gone over to intemperance by taking drink medicinally. Medical testimony now showed that the idea that drink could be taken medicinally with benefit was an exploded fallacy. In urging her hearers to join the temperance army she said that every other evil would tumble clown when the land in which they lived became sober. (Applause.) During the evening an enjoyable musical programme was submitted by the Legh-street Quartette party, (Miss A. Woodland, Miss L. Snelling, Mr. J. Corrin and Mr. A. Spruce.)
"MIND YOUR OWN BUSINESS."

The concluding meeting was held on Thursday even- ing when there was a crowded attendance, the Rev. J. F. Matthews presiding. The CHAIRMAN said no one could look upon the work of the 1.0.G.T. without being delighted to find they had been consistent in their attitude on the temperance question. They had so many panaceas advocated for intemperance that it was like a breath of ozone to find one or two societies taking a strong and consistent attitude against the tendency to municipalize the drink traffic. If 15,000 doctors were scientifically correct, drink was a poison and ought to be labelled as such and he was the last man in creation to hold up a hand for the municipalization of what the doctors con- demned. If he had given his allegiance to the Temperance Legislation League it was with a mental reservation against the disinterested management which they advocated. The liquor traffic was run on business principles and as no sound business man would run the traffic without a profit how could they have disinterested management? He hoped theylwould realize that the only thing to be done with the drink traffic was to have done with it altogether. (Applause). Mrs. WALKER, who had a hearty reception, delivered an address on "Mind your own business." People often said, she stated, "if people drink let them drink. It is not my business as they are not drinking my money." Those people were wrong. It was their con- cern. Did they ever think how many police we had in England and that the number was so large because they ss ere very largely publicans' porters kept to do the work rendered necessary by the drink traffic ? We could do with half the number of police if it were not for the drink traffic. Then we had our gaols filled, as the judges said,largely by people whose crimes were the result of drink, and the same thing applied to the asylums and workhouses which also had to be main- tained out of the public purse. In England we were very proud of our hospitals and these were without doubt very excellent institutions but it did not require much observation to prove that a large number of the patients were there either directly or indirectly as the result of taking intoxicating drink,and that if we had no liquor traffic our hospitals instead of being filled would be almost empty. (Hear, hear). What a change would take place if the people would make it their business to deal with the liquor traffic instead of saying it was not their business. (Applause). She had been asked "Do you think the liquor traffic is ever going to be swept away ?" Of course she did. She would not be there that night if she did not and the whole of the temperance sentiment of to-day was based upon the expectation that in the fulness of time England would be free from that terrorising power. (Applause). What was their business? To relieve the suffering and the poverty of the nation? Undoubtedly, and they as temperance people claimed that they were doing that. Poverty in the nation ought to be unknown and hunger would be a word foreign to our vocabulary if it were not for the liquor traffic. They did not say that all poverty existed through drink but they did say that a very great majority of the people were poor because in their youth they had wasted their substance in drink, and that if it had not been for the drink traffic there would not be so much squalor and filth, debt and difficulty which so many had to face. Poverty did not mean dirt, and if people were sober they would keep their self-respect. (Hear, hear.) The sober man with 255. a week was much better off than the man with 355. who took drink. Niost important of all, however, they had to realise that the liquor traffic was a danger to the rising generation and it was their duty to look after the youth of the land. They claimed that it was their business to free men and women from the power of strong drink and to give them that which would make life worth living, and by God's help they would do that. (Applause).

The Examiner, Saturday, January 19, 1907. NOTES ON GAMES AND SOCIALIST DEMONSTRATION' ATHLETICS. AT WARRINGTON. MR. PHILIP SNOWDEN, M.P., AND THE WORK OF THE SESSION. What He Claims for the I.L.P. Considerable interest was taken in a Socialist demonstration promoted by the Warrington branch of the Independent Labour Party and held in the Parr Hall on Saturday. Notwithstanding the fact that charges were made for admission: there was a good attendance. The principal speakers were Mr. Philip Snowden P., one of the most prominent figures in the SocialistM. world, Mrs. K. Bruce Glasier, 8.A., and Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P. for Newton division, Prior to the meeting selections were given on the organ by Mr. W. Pearce and were much appreciated. Mr. R. Pierce Williams presided and was supported on the platform by Mr. Philip Snowden, M.P., Mr. J. A. Seddon, M.P., Mrs. K. Bruce Glasier, the Rev. J. F. Matthews, Councillors F. Stott and J. Ball, Mr. Turner (Irlain Urban Council), Mrs. Wilkinson (Warrington Board of (uardians), and Messrs. T. Plumb (president Trades Council), E. Horrocks (president L.R.C.), J. Haley (Distress Committee), J. Hampson (secretary Right-to-Work Committee), E. Bagot, G Reeves, E. Randles, E. Highley and others. Socialist hymns were sung with great enthusiasm. The CHAIRMAN said the promoters of the meeting made no secret of the fact that it was a Socialist demonstration. (Applause.) The Independent Labour Party was avowedly a Socialist organization and its method was frankly independent representation. It I was significant of the conservatism, conscious or other- wise, of the English workingman that it should be necessary to justify to him the existence of a party formed primarily in his interests and which ought to be his peculiar medium for the expression of his political and social ideals. What work was there for the Inde- pendent Labour Party to do that either the Liberal party or the Tory party would not do ? One of the most outstanding features of the present situation was the existence of intense social and industrial evils—evils that prevailed to such an extent as to seriously affect the very lives of a large section of the people and this despite the fact that two great and experienced political parties had for a long time alternately controlled the legislative machine. The reason was that these parties had never attempted to bring about the fundamental change which Socialists believed was essential to a real and perma- nent improvement. Their efforts had been directed rather towards the mitigation of the evils, without attempting to erradicate the root cause—our wrong economic system. (Applause.) Socialists emphatically declared that unless they put away the present system of capitalism those evils in essence remained. The Independent Labour Party deserved well at the hands of every sincere social reformer. They had quickened the interest of the people in social questions and given an impetus to social reform. Their ultimate object was the brotherhood of man. (Applause). MR. SNOWDEN'S SPEECH. Mr. PHILIP SNOWDEN, ALP., who had a cordial reception, said that on previous occasions when he visited Warringten he came as a mere irresponsible agitator; now he had laid upon his shoulders something of the responsibility of statesman- ship. (Laughter and applause.) Nobody, he thought, could deny the ability and success with , which the Socialist party had carried on its work ' of social reform agitation, and he was full of faith that they would prove equally competent in the new, higher, and more responsible and dignified sphere into which they had been called. They recognized that it was , now expected, seeing that they had something of an opportunity, that they would be able to prove as legis- lators something of the practicability and the possibility of the ideals they had placed before the people.. (Applause.) Their object was through legislation to effect a social change which they described by the name of Socialism. The Independent Labour Party had never tried to hide the fact that it was a Socialist organization ; but if one had believed the newspapers for a few months after the results of the last election, one might have been inclined to believe that the Independent Labour Party had during all the• years of its existence been seeking in ways that were dark and by tricks that were mean to hide the fact that it was a Socialist party masquerading in the guise of a Labour party. The fact that the newspapers and orthodox politicians were ignorant of the fact that they were Socialists was cetainly not their (the Socialists') fault, for from a thousand street corners, from platforms wherever they could got the opportunity, they had for twelve or fifteen years, in season and out of season, been preaching to the people of this country that there was no possibility of any real and permanent improvement in their indus- trial and social conditions except in Socialism. (Applause.) He made that declaration to them again that night. Legislation could do nothing to lighten their toil and make life briqhter, except in so far as legislation embodied the principle of Socialism in prac- tice. A good deal of admiration had been expressed for the legislative programme of THE LATE SESSION 01, _PARLIAMENT. To those who had simply the old idea of legislation which could see no further than mere tinkering at the existing machine, there was reason for satisfaction at the legislative achievements of the last nine months. It was perfectly true to say that there had never been. within this generation at least, a Session of Parlia- ment so productive of beneficial legislation as the last session. (Applause.) He was not there to claim the entire credit for the beneficial legislation of the Session as the exclusive work of the Labour party—he hoped he was not fool or knave enough to do that—but he believed he was perfectly justified in claiming that the legislative programme achieved would not have been what it was if it had not been for the presence of the' Independent Labour Party in Parliament. (Applause.) He had often appealed to the Liberal workingmen who had not the courage to separate themselves from old political associations but who sincerely wanted reform, that in their own interets as reformers, while retaining their faith in their own political party, the best thing they could do was to stimulate that party by putting into Parliament the influence of an independent Labour group. (Hear, hear.) He had never held that all the virtne and political intelligence of the country was inside the Labour and Socialist party. They had alway been ready to admit that there were in the Tory patty as well as in the Liberal party many men who DEPLORED AS SINCERELY AS SOCIALISTS deplored the existence of so much misery and ignorance in the land and men who in their hearts were quite as anxious as Socialists that something should be done to lessen the volume of misery and make the lives of the people happy. Socialists had never denied the existence of this sympathy and of this desire in the hearts of others. Where they had differed had been not in the heart but in the head. Socialists claimed to understand more clearly the character of this misery which they all equally deplored. They claimed, partly as the result of a closer and more intimate knowledge of working class conditions and partly as the result of a more or less scientific investigation, to understand the plan that ought to be followed and the legislation that might to be attempted in order to deal effectively with those conditions. Nothing could have justified their claim more emphatically and conclusively than the experience of the late session of Parliament. In the industrial legislation of that Session the PRACTICAL EXPERIENCE AND KNOWLEDGE of the Labour members had been simply invaluable in transforming the moderate legislation of the Govern- ment into measures of a far more practical and beneficial character. They must not for a moment imagine that a succession of sessions productive of the same character of legislation was going to be sufficient to satisfy the demands of the Labour party. (Applause.) They had got their Trades Disputes Bill and their Workmen's Compensation Act but industrial conditions remained just as they were before; employment was as difficult to get and to keep; wages were as low ; housing conditions were as bad and exactly the same number of paupers were still in the lend. These 'measures were mere palliatives. They had not touched in the slightest degree the root cause of the industrial and social misery of the people. He woefully misunder- stood the purpose for which the Labour Party had been sent to Parliament if that purpose was simply to prop up the existing industrial and social system, to plaster the sore and palliate the suffering. No Labour Party was
NVORTItY TO BE CALLED A _LABOUR PARTY

or was worthy of the support of the workers of this country, which was not a Socialist party. (Applause.) Let those who believed in what they called Labour representative disavow as much as they would a con- fession of Socialist faith. They could not help them- selves; they were making a Socialist programme the programme of their anti-Socialist party. fie had never had a desire to impose his Socialism or the Socialism of the Independent Labour Party upon all those who were willing to co-operate with them, lie had such faith in the converting power of Socialism that he could afford to wait until those men were convinced by the force of an intelligent conviction—and that con- viction was rapidly coming over the minds of the intelli- gent men and women of this country who wanted to use political power for a practical purpose. It was only by removing the economic

SUBJECTION OF THE \YORKERS TO MONOPOLY that an improvement in their condition could be effected. Mr. Lloyd George admitted that the Board of Trade returns disclosed the fact that from 1900 to 1905 in each and all ot those years the wages of the working people had been going down. The returns of his department, however, showed that during the same period the volume of trade, or in other words the volume of wealth pro- duced, had been annually increasing. Every year the disparity between the amount of wealth the workers produced and what they got' for their own use and enjoyment was getting wider and wider. The Government returns conclusively proved where and to whom that wealth was going. On investigating the Inland Revenue returns for twenty years he came across the striking fact that between 1884 and 189 i the gross amount of income assessed for income tax did not increase by 70 million pounds whereas in the following ten years it increaled by 210

million pounds. In each ten years the income tax was practically from the same people—a million in number. Therefore during the last ten years these million people had been grower richer at a rate five times more rapidy than they did in the preceding ten years. (" Shame "). The power by which these people were able to get rich so much more rapidly was due to the fact that they possessed a monopoly of the means of creating wealth. Therefore it needed no argument that if this monopoly was the cause of the riches of the few and the conse- quent poverty of the many,it was only by attacking that monopoly that those inequalities of wealth dis- tribution would be altered. (Applause.) The effect of Factory and Public Health legislation was to make the workers stronger and able to produce more; conse- quently they made more profits for the employing class, but competition kept their wages down. A significant and important fact was that the competition for employment was causing increased intensity of exist- ence. A large Lancashire cotton spinner told him that within the last few years the average life of a Lancashire cotton spinner had shortened by ten years. We were

gap.desc: skipped/gap: fewer than 20 non-control characters after cleanup

div.head: USING MEN UP MORE RAPIDLY
div.p: USING MEN UP MORE RAPIDLY

to-day than ever we did and their wages during their working life were only sufficient to keep them from week to week. The result was that for those who were unfortunate enough to live to old age there was a longer period of pauperised existence in store for them. Dealing with the orthodox political parties, Mr. Snowden said the principle of Toryism was the govern- ment of the people by an aristocracy for the good of the people—(laughter)—treating the people as having no rights but regarding the aristocracy as having certain obligations to treat them fairly well. The principle of Liberalism was individual freedom and the idea of Liberalism Nuts that indi- vidual freedom could be best attained by giving to every individual the utmost liberty to fight against everybody else having any individual liberty,. (Laugh- ter.) The Labour party was democratic. It knew no sections and no class and regarded the people as a unit, as an organism, as one, the real and true interests of all being identical. Dealing with the rise of the Labour party Mr. Snowden contended it was due to the fact that Liberalism failed to recognize the character of the work required to be done under the changed con- ditions of later years.

div.head: I'ROGRESS WOULD NOT WAIT
div.p: I'ROGRESS WOULD NOT WAIT

indefinitely, and If the instrument; to 'carry out the work of progress were not there, progress I would make its own instruments. That was what progress did when it made the political Labour 1 and Socialist party of this country. (Applause.) Under present conditions, the practice of human brotherhood was an impossibility. Socialists were I engaged in a winning fight and he believed that much sooner than many people imagined, they would see great changes. Competition' like every evil thing, contained the germs of its own destruction. (Applause.) They wanted public opinion, continued Mr. Snowden, to say to Parliament that a millionaire was a bigger disgrace to a nation than a pauper. A millionaire was a danger to society and himself, and society would save the millionaire against himself. They wanted public opinion to say that the enormous increases of wealth produced by the labour of the people should not go into the possession of a mere handful and that they must have a Land Bill which would abolish the curse of landlordism. (Applause.) When public opinion had awakened, they would in one short generation by intelligent legislation transform the face of England and make it a country that would be indeed great, not in the extent of its empire but in the happiness, contentment, and well- being of its people. (Applause). "OUR GREATEST STATESMAN." Mrs. BRUCE GLASIER then delivered a stirring address in whibh she alluded to Mr. Kier Hardie as "the greatest statesman alive to-day." Continuing she said the present system of society was unjust as the power of the landlord and the capitalist sucked the money away from the workers. (Applause). WHAT TO DO WITH THE HOUSE OF LORDS. Mr. J. A. SEDDON, said Socialists believed that the means of production, distribution and exchange should be in the hands of the whole of the people to be used for the people. Mr. Chamberlain in 1884 said that every man born into this country had a right in the land by birth. What ransom, he added, were the present holders going to pay to the disinherited? Socialists were more generous than Mr. Chamberlain. They did not ask for ransom but said "Hand over what does not belong to you and no questions will be asked." (Laughter and applause.) It might be said that the present holders did not steal it. He granted that but it was an axiom of common law that the receiver of stolen property was worse than the thief.(Applause.) He ( nr.Seddon)had been asked repeatedly what he would do with the House of Lords and he had replied " Send them to Madame Tussauds." (Laughter.) The House of Lords would exist as long as the people permitted it and no longer.(Applause.) Mr. Smidon then condemned ccinpetition and said that Socialists were striving for international brotherhood and peace. Every man who was willing to work ought to have the right to work and when he had contributed to the communal wealth, he should sit down, as his natural, economic and divine right, at the banquet of life and partake of the good things that came from our communal life. (Applause). I They looked forward to the time when men would actu- ally turn their swords into plough shares and pruning hooks, for the democracy in this country and in other countries had no quarrel. (Applause). The Rev. J. F'. MArrutEws moved a vote of thanks to the speakers and chairman. Alluding to 'Ars), Bruce Glasier, he said he would like to see one or two women in Parliament. It would be a very fine thing to see them thrash out some of that legislation in favour of the women of our country. (Applause). The vote was heartily aceordea and the meeting con- cluded.

Hickman Mason, Mr. and Mrs. James Mason, Mrs. Brough, the presided at the organ. . managers of Padgate School, his playmates in Standard LECTURE ON " TENNYSON." I. Mrs. C. Grounds, Mrs. T. Weston, Mr. and Mrs. On ?Monday evening a lecture on "The secret of D'ennett, Mr. and. Mrs. T. Boyd, Mr. and Mrs. J. Monks. Tennyon s charm " was delivered in the schoolroom by and Miss Bolton. Mr. J. Anthony Barnes, B.A. There was a good attend- ance, Mr. W. Silcock presiding and being supported on the platform by the Rev. J. Manning. The Chairman said he did not know of any among the English poets who appealed more powerfully to our race than Tenny- son and Browning. While, however, Browning appealed more to the intellect, Tennyson touched the heart and there was a wonderful rhythm, grace, and beauty in his poems, Mr. 11A RNES dealt with his subject in an able and highly interesting manner. He pointed out that like many other good things, the love of poetty was often an acquired taste which was not born until one was fairly well on in life. On reading Tennyson, one could not but be struck with the haunting rhythm of his music. He voiced the whole conflict of the last century in its craving for light and truth. He lived in obscurity, his life being almost that of a recluse. ' Dealing with poetry in general, the lecturer sail the poet differed from the ordinary mortal in that he could see in this world with all its change and experiences an indefinable harmony and beauty and he could use the common instrument of speech to grasp and express , those vague, dim, evanescent emotions within us which were too faint and elusive to rise to the surface. He also gave expression to • the feelings which were too powerful and overwhelming for us to , find words in which to voice them. Tennyson was a close and careful observer of all that was going on in the world, and especially in the world of nature. To him nature was not something scientific, merely to be analysed and studied, but it was pervaded by a spirit and was always responsive to the moods of the man who looked upon it. The lecturer then quoted passages showing how Tennyson regarded nature, love, patriotism and religion. Dealing with the latter, he said Tennyson's attitude was never that of the man who Spojt as from the unseen with a message of certainty to is fellows' but was that of the man who cried from his heart to the unseen to see if there might be any response. There was no certainty or dogmatism in his writing on religion but a sense of some Power to which he could speak and which was friendly to man. The lecturer quoted many choice extracts from the poet's works and recited with fine effect "The charge of the Light Brigade" and "Crossing the Bar." • Mr. FRANK A. HARRIS moved a vote of thanks to tbe Lecturer and Chairman, and spoke of the educational force which lay behind the lecture. Mr. KENNEDY seconded, and the motion was supported by the Rev. IV. H. MosTLEY (Prodsbam) and the -Rev. J. MANNING. The audience, who it was evident thoroughly appre- ciated the lecture, accorded the vote with great hearti- ness.

" Memnon " in " Dawn " has a word or two about the House of Lords, for whose future he clearly fears. " Memnon " is candid enough to say, however, " like every Conservative who has the power to use the brains which God presumably once gave him, I cannot logically justify a body based, in the main, upon hereditary privilege in a day of democratic rights." * * * The Education Committee recommends that the " People's College "be in future called" Warrington Brewtnall School " and suggests this name to the Board of Education. Apparently the school managers have been somnolent, for nothing has been heard from them as to the change in the name of the old school. * * * Real friendship is a slow grower.—" Chesterfield." He is rich whose income exceeds his expenses.— " Bruyere." Nioney is like Manure—of very little use except it be spread.—" Bacon." A fool and his words are soon parted. —" Shenstone." Women and music should never be dated.— " Goldsmith." By taking a second wife a man pays a compliment to the first, showing that she made him happy,— "Dr. Johnson." * * How unreliable press telegrams from abroad sometimes are is illustrated by a paragraph published in the "Evening News" on Thursday. The para- graph consisted of two telegrams the first of which described a carriage accident in the South of France and stated that " the Princess Lubomirski received such grave injuries that her recovery is impossible." This must have been very terrifying reading for the friends of the Princess, but fiva lines lower down they would see—if they were not too overcome—that a second telegram from another source reported that "the Princess is not believed to be gravely injured." The next telegram will probably say either that the Princess is dead, or that the accident never happened. * * * We are occasionally amused by the queer drawings called by the" Dawn" "cartoons for the people." What " the neople " think of them would be inter- esting if" the people " saw them. The one in the current number pictures John Bull sailing along con- tentedly in a small boat with a somewhat bibulous- looking " C. 8." at the helm. Right ahead are the cliffs of "Ruin " and jagged rocks la'belled "Unemployment," " Disunion," " Loss of the Colonies," etc. There is more than one conclusion to be drawn from the picture. We should imagine that John Bull looks quite content to risk all these terrors of the deep because his is the good ship " Cobdenism "and is fanned by the strong breeze of "trade returns." That, however, is not the idea the " Dawn " intends to convey
